2. Pregnant women with Type 1 Diabetes in a longitudinal observational study investigating preeclampsia risk prediction during the second and third trimesters.
Effect Summary:

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. Sport Implications: The provided findings do not have an athletic context. The study population was pregnant women with Type 1 Diabetes, and the outcome investigated was preeclampsia. Biomarker: 1,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D / Vitamin D Binding Protein Ratio
Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This longitudinal, prospective observational study investigated the predictive value of vitamin D metabolites and their ratios for preeclampsia in women with Type 1 Diabetes during pregnancy (second and third trimesters).
Effect Summary: In women with Type 1 Diabetes, elevated 1,25(OH)2D/VDBP ratios were significantly associated with and predictive of subsequent preeclampsia (PE) in the second (~22 weeks) and third (~32 weeks) trimesters of pregnancy. Specifically, higher ratios were observed in T1DM women who developed PE compared to normotensive T1DM women. At ~22 weeks gestation, every unit increase in the ratio increased the odds of developing PE by almost three-fold (OR: 2.71, p=0.009), with similar odds at ~32 weeks (OR: 2.53, p=0.013).
Sport Implications: The provided findings describe the association of the 1,25-Dihydroxyvitamin D / Vitamin D Binding Protein ratio with preeclampsia risk in pregnant women with Type 1 Diabetes. This context is entirely unrelated to athletic populations, training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: Recreationally trained women, including naturally cycling women and oral contraceptive (OC) users, underwent an acute intervention involving oral N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation (total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ body mass) or a placebo. Effect Summary: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation did not statistically change 1-km cycling time trial completion time compared to placebo. Completion times were statistically equivalent between the placebo and NAC trials for both naturally cycling women and women using oral contraceptives. There was also no significant difference in completion time between these two groups.
Sport Implications: 1-km time trial completion time serves as a direct and practical performance diagnostic, reflecting anaerobic power and capacity crucial for short-to-medium duration cycling events. These findings indicate that acute high-dose N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation, when administered prior to and during a combined fixed-intensity cycling and all-out 1-km time trial protocol, does not provide an ergogenic benefit for this specific performance metric in recreationally trained women, irrespective of their oral contraceptive use. Therefore, athletes and coaches should not expect performance improvements in similar cycling events from acute NAC supplementation under these conditions.

Activity Context Summary: Female team-sport athletes participated in post-exercise nutritional interventions. Exercise protocols included either repeated simulated team games (involving intermittent running, sprints, agility, and jumps) or a protocol designed to induce muscle damage through repeated maximal sprinting and plyometric jumps. The nutritional intervention involved consuming 500 mL of either cow's milk or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution immediately post-exercise.
Effect Summary: One study (ID: 31906239) reported that post-exercise consumption of 500 mL of cow's milk attenuated losses in 10m sprint performance (effect size = 0.30 to 0.53) following the first simulated team game, compared to an energy-matched carbohydrate solution. However, overall performance remained below baseline at 96 hours. For 15m sprint, within-group increases were observed for both milk and carbohydrate groups from the first to the second simulated team game, but between-group comparisons were unclear. Another study (ID: 29462969) found that the effect of post-exercise milk consumption versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on 10m sprint time was unclear following a protocol designed to induce muscle damage.
Sport Implications: 10-meter sprint performance is a direct measure of explosive power, acceleration, and short-distance speed, which are critical components of performance in many team sports. Monitoring this biomarker helps assess an athlete's recovery status and readiness for subsequent training or competition. The findings suggest that milk might contribute to attenuating initial decrements in 10m sprint performance after an acute bout of strenuous team-sport activity, potentially aiding in acute recovery. However, the evidence is inconsistent regarding milk's superior effect over an energy-matched carbohydrate solution for comprehensive or sustained recovery of sprint performance. Therefore, while 10m sprint performance is highly relevant for assessing recovery and performance capacity, the specific impact of milk as a recovery aid, beyond a basic carbohydrate solution, on this particular metric requires further clarification.

Activity Context Summary: The studies involved healthy, well-trained participants and resistance-trained males. Interventions included a single bout of intensive resistance training designed to induce muscle damage, followed by a single dose of Cannabidiol (CBD) or placebo, and three consecutive days of high-intensity, high-volume resistance training (barbell back squat protocol) followed by post-exercise branched chain amino acid and carbohydrate (BCAA-CHO) or carbohydrate-only (CHO) supplementation.
Effect Summary: Following an intensive resistance training protocol, 1RM Squat strength consistently decreased, indicating muscle fatigue and damage. One study observed that after a single intensive bout, 1RM Back Squat strength significantly decreased at 24 hours in both CBD and placebo groups. However, after 72 hours, the CBD group demonstrated significant recovery and a slight increase in performance compared to placebo, following an overall linear recovery trend. Another study involving three consecutive days of high-intensity resistance training found similar decrements in 1RM squat strength in both BCAA-CHO and CHO supplementation groups, with BCAA-CHO not mitigating these performance reductions.
Sport Implications: 1RM Squat strength serves as a critical performance diagnostic tool for assessing an athlete's maximal lower body strength and its recovery trajectory following intense training. Significant decreases in 1RM Squat performance directly indicate acute training stress, muscle damage, and neuromuscular fatigue. The rate of recovery of 1RM Squat strength can signal the effectiveness of recovery strategies and the athlete's adaptive response to training load. Sustained decrements suggest insufficient recovery or potential underrecovery, while a quicker return to baseline or an increase in 1RM indicates successful recovery and potential positive adaptation. The findings suggest that interventions like CBD might support faster maximal strength recovery after intense, damage-inducing exercise, whereas certain BCAA-CHO formulations may not be effective in attenuating performance decrements during periods of high training volume and insufficient recovery time.

Activity Context Summary:
Studies investigated 20-meter sprint time in various athletic contexts:
-   Semi-professional male soccer players recovering from prolonged, intermittent sprint activity, with Montmorency tart cherry concentrate supplementation.
-   Elite male soccer players monitored over a 12-week competitive period, including uncongested and congested match play phases.
-   Female team-sport athletes recovering from exercise-induced muscle damage following a repeated sprinting and jumping protocol, with post-exercise milk or carbohydrate drink interventions.
Effect Summary:
Observed effects on 20-meter sprint time were:
-   Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) supplementation led to significantly faster 20m sprint times (4%) at 48 hours post-exercise compared to placebo in semi-professional soccer players recovering from intermittent sprints.
-   In elite male soccer players, sprint times showed mixed changes across competitive periods: a moderate increase (slower time, ES = 0.62) from baseline to an uncongested match play period, followed by a moderate decrease (faster time, ES = -0.76) from the uncongested to a congested match play period. Most players ultimately achieved faster times after the congested period compared to baseline and the uncongested period.
-   For female team-sport athletes recovering from exercise-induced muscle damage, the effect of post-exercise milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on 20m sprint performance recovery was unclear, with no clear advantage observed for either intervention.
Sport Implications:
The 20-meter sprint time is a crucial performance diagnostic and a sensitive indicator of recovery and fatigue in athletes. It directly reflects an athlete's maximal acceleration and short-distance speed, which are vital components in many team sports and sprint-based activities.

Changes in 20-meter sprint performance can signal the effectiveness of recovery strategies, such as nutritional interventions like Montmorency tart cherry concentrate, which was shown to accelerate functional performance recovery post-sprint activity. This suggests it can be used to monitor the efficacy of recovery protocols.

Fluctuations in sprint times can also serve as an indicator of training load and competitive stress. The observation of varied sprint performance across different match play periods (uncongested vs. congested) in elite soccer highlights its utility in monitoring the adaptive responses or accumulated fatigue due to varying training and competitive loads. A decrease (faster time) can indicate positive adaptation or optimal recovery, while an increase (slower time) suggests fatigue, under-recovery, or potential overreaching, helping coaches adjust training intensity or recovery emphasis. However, the study on elite soccer players showed complex changes, suggesting that context (e.g., initial fatigue, adaptive responses to increased competitive load) is critical for interpretation.

An unclear effect of a recovery intervention (milk vs. carbohydrate) on 20m sprint time suggests that while other markers of muscle function might improve, sprint speed recovery can be more resistant to change or require more potent interventions or longer observation periods to demonstrate clear differences. Overall, 20-meter sprint time is a highly relevant performance diagnostic for assessing training adaptation, monitoring recovery status, and managing overall athlete load.

Activity Context Summary:
The findings include studies on young elite soccer players during a one-year training cycle, observing seasonal changes, sunlight exposure, and the effects of 8-week vitamin D supplementation. Another study involved elite male rowers undergoing multiple strenuous, non-weight-bearing training sessions, with an assessment of general health status. Additionally, there was a study on physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake participating in 12 weeks of walking exercise training combined with daily protein supplementation.

Non-athletic contexts reported include: children with Noonan Syndrome; children with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia during chemotherapy; patients with Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (MRONJ) receiving teriparatide and oral vitamin D; women at risk of vitamin D deficiency undergoing a 12-week food-based vitamin D fortification intervention; and pregnant women with Type 1 Diabetes for preeclampsia risk prediction. These non-athletic contexts are not directly relevant to exercise physiology or athletic performance.
Effect Summary:
Serum/plasma 25-Hydroxyvitamin D levels in young elite soccer players exhibited significant seasonal variations, being significantly higher in summer (August) and considerably lower during autumn-winter (December-May). A short-term 8-week vitamin D supplementation (5,000 IU/day) did not produce a sustained extended effect on levels, with changes primarily dictated by sunlight radiation. Deficiency (≤20 ng/dl) was widespread in autumn-winter, affecting up to 25% of participants.

In elite male rowers, 30% of the study sample presented with insufficient 25-Hydroxyvitamin D levels, coinciding with an annual seasonal nadir for vitamin D.

In physically active older adults engaged in 12 weeks of walking exercise, serum 25-Hydroxyvitamin D concentrations increased in both protein-supplemented and placebo groups, indicating an effect of physical activity or associated factors like sun exposure, but no difference was observed between the groups.

In non-athletic contexts: levels were unchanged in children with Noonan Syndrome compared to controls, though a high prevalence of insufficiency/deficiency was noted within the cohort. Levels were lower than normal at diagnosis and dropped significantly during chemotherapy in children with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia. Oral vitamin D supplementation (1,000 IU/day) led to significantly increased 25-Hydroxyvitamin D levels post-treatment in patients with MRONJ. A 12-week food-based vitamin D fortification (30 µg/day) significantly increased levels in women during winter, while placebo groups saw a decrease. Pregnant women with Type 1 Diabetes showed a higher frequency of deficiency/insufficiency compared to non-diabetics, but 25-Hydroxyvitamin D levels did not predict preeclampsia.
Sport Implications: 25-Hydroxyvitamin D status is a crucial aspect of athlete health and performance, particularly due to its significant seasonal fluctuations observed in athletes like young elite soccer players. The prevalence of deficiency/insufficiency during autumn and winter highlights a risk for impaired immune function and overall physiological well-being, which can negatively impact training consistency, adaptation, and performance. Continuous monitoring and strategic, potentially longer-term, supplementation may be necessary to maintain optimal levels, especially during periods of reduced sun exposure or increased training loads, as short-term supplementation may not yield sustained effects. The finding of insufficient levels in elite rowers underscores that this is a common nutritional concern in athletic populations. While acute calcium intake may mitigate exercise-induced bone resorption, underlying vitamin D insufficiency could compromise long-term bone health and increase the risk of bone stress injuries. In active populations, regular physical activity may contribute to maintaining adequate vitamin D status, likely through increased outdoor exposure. Therefore, monitoring 25-Hydroxyvitamin D levels can inform nutritional and training load management strategies to support athlete resilience, optimize recovery, and potentially enhance performance by maintaining robust immune function and bone health.

Activity Context Summary: The study involved 11 young healthy males undergoing two distinct heat stress protocols. One protocol involved exertional heating through cycling exercise at an intensity eliciting 60% VO2max in a 30°C room until rectal temperature reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. The other was exogenous heating via hot water immersion. The participants' training state beyond 'young healthy males' was not specified.
Effect Summary: Plasma 3-Hydroxykynurenine (3-HK) concentration showed a steady increase during the exertional heating (cycling) phase, which became more pronounced during the subsequent recovery phase, peaking at a rectal temperature of 38°C. This elevation was statistically significant (p < 0.001) and was observed exclusively in the exertional heating trial, not during the exogenous heating trial. The increase was transient, with concentrations generally returning to baseline during recovery, suggesting an adaptable physiological response. 3-HK is a metabolite within the kynurenine pathway, known for its pro-oxidant and excitotoxic properties.
Sport Implications: The increase in 3-Hydroxykynurenine during exertional heating, which combines exercise and heat stress, suggests that this biomarker reflects the acute physiological load associated with such demanding conditions. This is relevant for athletes training or competing in hot environments. The activation of the kynurenine pathway, indicated by elevated 3-HK, may be a response to the combined metabolic and thermal stress, potentially linking to increased oxidative stress given 3-HK's pro-oxidant nature. The transient nature of the increase and subsequent return to baseline implies an acute, adaptable response rather than chronic maladaptation. Monitoring 3-HK could potentially offer insights into the immediate stress response and recovery dynamics in athletes exposed to exertional heat, helping to understand the physiological cost of such training or competition. However, the study primarily frames KP metabolites as 'disease biomarkers,' and direct links to athletic performance enhancement or long-term adaptation remain to be established.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated the influence of fixed-intensity and sprint cycling, with or without acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation, on physiological responses in recreationally trained women (naturally cycling and oral contraceptive users). The other study was an observational assessment of sex-specific differences in older adults (women and men), focusing on oxi-inflammatory responses and cardiovascular health, without any athletic intervention or context.
Effect Summary: In recreationally trained women, 3-Nitrotyrosine blood plasma concentration significantly increased after 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling followed by an all-out 1-km sprint time trial, compared to baseline. This exercise-induced increase was observed in both naturally cycling women and women using oral contraceptives, and was not significantly affected by acute N-acetylcysteine supplementation. In an older adult population, higher serum 3-Nitrotyrosine concentrations were observed, particularly in older women, indicating reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and nitrosative stress. In men within this older adult cohort, it correlated with oxidized low-density lipoproteins (oxLDL).
Sport Implications: The observed exercise-induced increase in 3-Nitrotyrosine in recreationally trained women suggests its potential as a biomarker for monitoring acute training stress and the associated nitroxidative stress in athletes. Elevated levels indicate an acute physiological response involving reactive nitrogen species and subsequent protein nitration, reflecting the metabolic and cellular strain imposed by exercise. While this finding indicates a transient increase in stress following training load, the current studies do not provide sufficient information to determine its specific utility for fine-tuning training adaptations, predicting performance outcomes, or guiding precise recovery strategies beyond indicating the presence of acute nitroxidative stress. The study involving older adults has no direct athletic interpretation for training, recovery, or performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This observational study profiled metabolites in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients of varying disease severity (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls using NMR metabolomics.
Effect Summary: 4-hydroxyphenyl acetate showed metabolic changes in urine, with differences observed between Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients and Medical Ward COVID-19 patients.
Sport Implications: The findings are derived from a study investigating COVID-19 disease severity and metabolic profiles in affected patients versus healthy controls. There is no athletic population, training intervention, or performance outcome measured. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery.

Activity Context Summary: Healthy male and female cyclists participated in a 2-week dietary supplementation period with either high (20 g/d) or low (5 g/d) doses of hemp fiber or a placebo. Each supplementation period culminated in a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max. Biomarker levels were measured post-exercise.
Effect Summary: Plasma levels of 4-methoxycinnamic acid were observed to be higher (VIP = 1.4) post-2.25 hours of intensive cycling, specifically after 2-week hemp fiber supplementation. It was identified as a methyl derivative of ferulic acid, a phenolic compound found in hemp fibers, and was part of an overall shift towards beneficial metabolite profiles.
Sport Implications: The increase in 4-methoxycinnamic acid post-intensive cycling, following hemp fiber supplementation, suggests its systemic bioavailability in athletes. As part of a beneficial metabolite profile and a plant-derived phenolic compound, it indicates potential contributions to antioxidant or anti-inflammatory effects, which are critical for an athlete's recovery and adaptation processes after strenuous exercise. This biomarker could therefore serve as an indicator of the absorption and metabolic processing of specific dietary compounds that may support recovery and mitigate exercise-induced inflammation, thereby influencing an athlete's training adaptation and overall performance capacity through improved metabolic and inflammatory responses.

Activity Context Summary: The study investigated the effects of 4-week oral garlic extract supplementation (1000 mg/day) on 40-km cycling time trial performance in healthy adult males. The intervention was a single-blind crossover design.
Effect Summary: 40-km cycling time trial performance was not significantly improved (p > 0.05) after 4 weeks of 1000 mg/day oral garlic supplementation. The mean performance time in the garlic trial was 81.18 ± 2.12 min compared to 84.14 ± 2.88 min in the placebo trial.
Sport Implications: The 40-km cycling time trial is a direct and highly relevant performance diagnostic tool for assessing endurance capacity in cycling. The findings indicate that 4-week oral garlic supplementation, at the dose tested, does not enhance this specific measure of endurance performance in healthy adult males. While the study observed attenuated oxidative stress, inflammatory response, and some markers of muscle damage, these physiological improvements did not translate into a measurable performance benefit in the context of this demanding cycling challenge. This suggests that for athletes or individuals aiming to improve 40-km cycling performance, garlic supplementation, as administered, may not be an effective training or recovery aid for direct performance enhancement, even if it might modulate other markers related to stress or recovery.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study aimed to identify genetic susceptibility loci for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) in a general population, including EOC cases, controls, and BRCA1/2 mutation carriers. It involved genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and meta-analysis to assess genetic risk factors.
Effect Summary: A genetic variant at the 4q26 locus (specifically the lead SNP rs635634, located upstream of the ABO gene) is associated with a significantly higher genetic risk of all invasive epithelial ovarian cancer in a meta-analysis. SYNPO2 (myopodin), a gene near this locus, is functionally involved in actin filament organization, cell motility, and growth, with a reported tumor suppressor role, while the ABO gene determines blood group and is linked to pancreatic cancer risk. This locus contributes to EOC susceptibility.
Sport Implications: The findings exclusively pertain to identifying genetic predisposition for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer in a non-athletic, clinical risk prediction context. There is no information provided that links the 4q26 locus, or the genes SYNPO2 and ABO, to athletic training stress, recovery, adaptation, performance, or exercise-induced physiological responses relevant to sports medicine. Therefore, this biomarker, as presented, does not offer insights for sports-science applications or athlete monitoring.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigates molecular determinants of hemogenic endothelial cells and hematopoietic progenitor cells using human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) and mouse embryos, focusing on endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT) and the generation of functional hematopoietic stem cells in vitro.
Effect Summary: In human embryonic stem cell blood differentiation experiments, NT5E (CD73) gene transcript and cell surface protein expression was observed to be lower (downregulated) in GATA2/eGFP+ hemogenic endothelial cells (HECs) but upregulated in GATA2/eGFP- non-hemogenic endothelial cells (ECs).
Sport Implications: The provided findings describe the role of CD73 in the differentiation of endothelial cell populations from human embryonic stem cells and in mouse embryos. This context is specific to developmental biology and cellular differentiation, with no direct relevance to training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: The study involved endurance athletes, including trained and untrained subgroups. The intervention consisted of two identical 60-minute continuous endurance running field tests (RFTs). Each RFT involved 40 minutes of running at 95% of Heart Rate (HR) at Individual Anaerobic Threshold (IAT), followed by 20 minutes at 110% of HR at IAT to induce exhaustion. Biomarkers were measured before, immediately after, 3 hours after, and 24 hours after each bout.
Effect Summary: Changes in 5-Bound Distance (as a blood-based biomarker) were observed over time following continuous endurance exercise bouts. It demonstrated excellent reliability (ICC > 0.90).
Sport Implications: As a blood-based biomarker, 5-Bound Distance indicates physiological exercise response and shows promise for monitoring athletes' training load and recovery processes, particularly after strenuous endurance exercise. Its excellent reliability suggests it could be a consistent measure for tracking acute responses to training and recovery.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study developed and validated a female-focused predictive atherosclerosis risk signature based on serum metabolites and clinical traits in patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), aiming to improve cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk assessment in this clinical population. The context involved observational diagnostics, not athletic training, performance, or recovery.
Effect Summary: A 5-feature score (comprising age, glycine, M-LDL-C, IDL-C, and omega-6/omega-3 ratio) was developed. This score accurately classified SLE patients with or without subclinical atherosclerosis, stratified distinct high and low subclinical atherosclerosis risk subgroups, and predicted 3-year atherosclerosis progression in female postpubertal patients with juvenile-onset SLE. The score was associated with elevated cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk.
Sport Implications: This biomarker and its associated predictive score are developed and validated in a clinical population (patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus) for the specific purpose of assessing and predicting subclinical atherosclerosis and general CVD risk in a disease context. The findings do not provide information relevant to understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in healthy athletes. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: Healthy male and female cyclists undergoing 2-week daily dietary supplementation with either high-dose (20 g/d) or low-dose (5 g/d) hemp hull powder, or a placebo. Each supplementation period concluded with a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max.
Effect Summary: Plasma levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) were observed to change as a key and significant metabolite within the tryptophan pathway, which was significantly influenced by high-dose hemp fiber supplementation combined with vigorous exercise.
Sport Implications: As a main metabolite of serotonin, changes in plasma 5-HIAA reflect altered serotonin turnover and metabolism. In the context of athletes undergoing intensive cycling and dietary intervention, these changes indicate an influence on the tryptophan pathway. Given serotonin's role in central fatigue, mood regulation, and sleep, alterations in 5-HIAA could potentially offer insights into aspects of neurophysiological response to training stress and dietary interventions, which are critical for an athlete's recovery and adaptation. However, this study did not directly link 5-HIAA changes to specific performance metrics or recovery markers, but rather identified it as part of broader metabolomic shifts influenced by exercise and supplementation.

Activity Context Summary: Healthy male and female cyclists undergoing 2 weeks of daily hemp fiber (5 or 20 g/d) or placebo supplementation, followed by a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout at approximately 70% VO2max. Plasma 5-Hydroxytryptophan was measured post-exercise.
Effect Summary: Plasma 5-hydroxytryptophan levels were increased post-2.25 hours of intensive cycling, particularly after 2-weeks of high-dose hemp fiber supplementation. This change was identified as part of a shift towards beneficial metabolite profiles and a significant influence on the tryptophan metabolic pathway.
Sport Implications: As a precursor to serotonin, an increase in 5-hydroxytryptophan post-intensive exercise, associated with dietary intervention, suggests an enhanced activity within the tryptophan metabolic pathway. This shift, described as part of beneficial metabolite profiles, could potentially indicate improved metabolic adaptation or support recovery processes in athletes, as serotonin plays roles in mood, sleep, and gut function, all crucial for an athlete's well-being and ability to adapt to training stress.

Activity Context Summary: The context involves UK military personnel recovering from lower limb musculoskeletal injuries, where persistent pain is a primary limiting factor. The intervention is a rehabilitation program comparing high-frequency, low-load Blood Flow Restriction Resistance Training (BFR-RT) at different limb occlusion pressures (40% vs. 80% LOP) and against usual care. The BFR-RT sessions involve unilateral leg press and knee extension exercises performed at 20% of 1-Repetition Maximum (1RM). This population is in a state of injury recovery rather than peak athletic performance training.
Effect Summary: This document is a study protocol, and no actual dose-response results or observed changes in 5-Repetition Maximum (5RM) are reported. The anticipated direction of change for 5RM, as an assessment of functional muscular strength, is an increase, indicating enhanced strength.
Sport Implications: While 5-Repetition Maximum (5RM) is a fundamental performance diagnostic in sports science, used for monitoring training adaptations, assessing muscular strength, and guiding rehabilitation and return-to-play decisions, this specific document is a study protocol and reports no observed findings. Therefore, no direct implications regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery can be drawn from the provided data. Generally, an increase in 5RM would signify improved functional strength, which is crucial for athletic performance, progression in training loads, and successful recovery from musculoskeletal injuries.

Activity Context Summary: Both studies involved female team-sport athletes and investigated post-exercise nutritional interventions. One study examined recovery following repeated simulated team games (intermittent running, sprints, agility, jumps) over a 48-hour period. The other study focused on recovery from a whole-body exercise protocol designed to induce muscle damage through repeated maximal sprints and plyometric jumps. In both cases, the intervention involved consuming either cow's milk or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution immediately post-exercise to assess their impact on recovery and performance.
Effect Summary: Post-exercise consumption of cow's milk, compared to an energy-matched carbohydrate solution, attenuated losses and promoted faster recovery of 5-meter sprint performance in female team-sport athletes. Specifically, milk consumption resulted in lower (faster) sprint times at 24 hours post-exercise (possible small benefit, ES = 0.45) following a muscle-damaging protocol. Similarly, following simulated team games, milk consumption attenuated losses in 5-meter sprint performance, particularly after the first game (possible-likely benefit, ES = 0.40 to 0.58). However, for many other time points or after repeated strenuous bouts, the effects of milk on 5-meter sprint performance were often unclear, and performance generally remained below baseline even at 72-96 hours post-exercise.
Sport Implications: 5-meter sprint performance is a direct measure of an athlete's acceleration and explosive power, crucial for team sports and other events requiring rapid changes in speed. The findings indicate that post-exercise nutritional strategies, such as cow's milk, can support the recovery of this critical performance metric, especially in the acute phase following strenuous exercise inducing muscle damage. Improved recovery of 5-meter sprint performance suggests enhanced readiness for subsequent training sessions or competition, which is vital for effective training load management and adaptation. Monitoring 5-meter sprint times can serve as a valuable performance diagnostic tool to assess an athlete's recovery status and identify potential under-recovery, thereby informing adjustments to training intensity or recovery interventions to optimize performance and prevent overtraining.

Activity Context Summary: This study investigates the effects of early spironolactone therapy in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) without clinical right ventricular failure. It is a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial protocol, not involving athletes or an exercise training context.
Effect Summary: In patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) without right ventricular failure, early spironolactone therapy is hypothesized to improve the 6-minute walk distance over 24 weeks. The 6-minute walk distance is a primary endpoint and is known to significantly decrease with worsening functional class in PAH patients.
Sport Implications: The findings of this study do not directly support athletic interpretation as the context is a clinical trial on patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), not athletes undergoing training, recovery, or performance assessment. While 6-minute walk distance is a general measure of submaximal exercise capacity, its application and interpretation in this context are for clinical disease management and prediction of clinical worsening in a compromised population, not for understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in healthy athletes.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated new genetic susceptibility loci for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) by performing a meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) involving general population EOC cases and controls, as well as BRCA1/2 mutation carriers. Functional genomic analyses were used to characterize identified loci.
Effect Summary: A genetic variant at the 6p22.1 locus (near GPX6), specifically the SNP rs116133110, was significantly associated with a higher risk of the serous epithelial ovarian cancer subtype (p=3.0 x 10^-8) in a comprehensive meta-analysis. This association was not significant for all invasive EOC types.
Sport Implications: The findings of this study do not support an athletic interpretation. The research is focused solely on identifying genetic risk factors for epithelial ovarian cancer susceptibility and provides no context or data related to training stress, adaptation, athletic performance, recovery, or any other aspect of exercise physiology in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: Healthy male and female cyclists undergoing a 2-week dietary intervention with high or low dose hemp fiber supplementation, concluding with a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max.
Effect Summary: Plasma 7-dehydrocholesterol levels changed significantly as a metabolite hit within the steroid biosynthesis pathway, which was influenced by high-dose hemp fiber supplementation in combination with vigorous exercise. This modulation indicates an effect on cholesterol and vitamin D synthesis pathways.
Sport Implications: 7-Dehydrocholesterol, as a precursor to cholesterol and vitamin D3, is involved in pathways critical for athletic adaptation and recovery. Cholesterol is foundational for steroid hormone synthesis (e.g., testosterone, cortisol), which are vital for anabolic processes, muscle repair, and stress responses to training. Vitamin D3 plays roles in bone health, immune function, and potentially muscle performance and recovery. The observed modulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol in athletes undergoing intensive exercise and dietary intervention suggests that nutritional strategies can impact key metabolic and endocrine pathways relevant to an athlete's capacity for adaptation, recovery, and overall physiological resilience to training stress. Monitoring such changes could offer insights into how dietary interventions influence an athlete's endocrine status and metabolic flexibility.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The documents discuss 8-OHdG in the context of Huntington's Disease progression and as a marker of oxidative stress and genotoxicity in gas station refueling workers exposed to BTEX compounds.
Effect Summary: 8-OHdG, a marker of oxidative DNA damage, was initially reported as elevated in individuals with Huntington's Disease in serum, plasma, and leukocytes, with plasma levels correlating with proximity to diagnosis. However, subsequent studies failed to replicate these findings due to high biological variability and confounding factors (stress, depression, smoking, low weight, pollution, diet). In another context, serum 8-OHdG was significantly higher in gas station refueling workers compared to office workers, reflecting increased oxidative DNA damage from occupational BTEX exposure. Interestingly, after controlling for various confounding factors (age, gender, years of exposure, smoking, and drinking habits), 8-OHdG levels were found to be significantly lower in refueling workers than in office workers in that specific study.
Sport Implications: The provided findings do not directly support an athletic interpretation. Neither study involves athletes, exercise interventions, training load monitoring, or recovery processes. While 8-OHdG is a marker of oxidative DNA damage, a process that can be influenced by exercise, the documents primarily highlight its significant variability and susceptibility to numerous confounding factors (e.g., stress, diet, environmental pollutants, smoking, age, gender). This inherent variability, as reported in non-athletic populations, suggests that its utility as a reliable biomarker for monitoring training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes would be challenging without specific, well-controlled athletic studies.

Activity Context Summary: Studies involved ultra-endurance (males and females) and well-trained male athletes undergoing acute exhaustive exercise protocols (combined cycling and treadmill to volitional exhaustion or incremental treadmill to failure). Contexts included assessing the impact of habitual dietary antioxidant intake and 1-week nutritional supplementation (tomato powder, isolated lycopene) on exercise-induced oxidative stress responses.
Effect Summary: Exhaustive exercise consistently elevates 8-isoprostane levels (a marker of lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress) in plasma or blood. This post-exercise increase is negatively correlated with higher total dietary antioxidant intake. Furthermore, 1-week supplementation with tomato powder significantly attenuates the post-exercise elevation of 8-isoprostane compared to placebo, whereas isolated lycopene supplementation does not show a significant effect.
Sport Implications: 8-Isoprostane is a valuable biomarker for monitoring exercise-induced oxidative stress and cellular damage, which are key components of overall training stress and contributors to fatigue and impaired recovery. The findings indicate that dietary strategies, particularly higher antioxidant intake or specific whole-food supplements like tomato powder, can modulate the body's response to acute exhaustive exercise by reducing lipid peroxidation. This suggests potential nutritional interventions to support recovery and adaptation by mitigating oxidative damage, thereby enhancing an athlete's capacity to handle training loads. Monitoring 8-isoprostane can help in assessing the efficacy of recovery strategies and nutritional support in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: This study involved recreationally-trained men performing high-intensity cycling. The intervention was acute pre-exercise nutritional supplementation with either homemade chicken broth (rich in histidine-containing dipeptides) or a placebo soup, administered 25-40 minutes prior to an 8-minute high-intensity cycling time trial.
Effect Summary: Acute pre-exercise ingestion of homemade chicken broth resulted in a significant 5.2% improvement in 8-minute time trial mean power output compared to placebo.
Sport Implications: 8-minute Time Trial Mean Power is a direct and robust measure of high-intensity exercise performance, reflecting an athlete's capacity to sustain high power output over a significant duration. This biomarker helps in performance diagnostics, allowing for the assessment of training effectiveness and the impact of nutritional strategies on competitive ability. A 5.2% improvement in mean power is substantial in an athletic context, indicating enhanced performance capacity. This finding suggests a potential acute nutritional strategy to improve high-intensity cycling performance, which could be relevant for competition or specific training sessions where peak performance is desired.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated genetic susceptibility loci for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) in general population EOC cases and controls, as well as BRCA1/2 mutation carriers, through a meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies.
Effect Summary: The 9q34.2 locus (near the ABO gene) was found to be associated with a statistically significant higher risk of all invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (p<5x10^-8) in a meta-analysis, including data from ovarian cancer cases, controls, and BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation carriers.
Sport Implications: The findings of this study focus exclusively on identifying genetic susceptibility loci for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer within a general population context. There is no reported athletic context, and therefore, this biomarker does not directly help understand training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. Its relevance is to disease risk prediction, not exercise physiology.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated critically ill adult COVID-19 patients receiving convalescent plasma therapy or usual care.
Effect Summary: APRIL (TNFSF13) levels were variable in subphenotype-1 of critically ill COVID-19 patients and were used as part of a panel to characterize three distinct immune subphenotypes. These subphenotypes predicted differential treatment responses to convalescent plasma therapy and clinical outcomes (hospital mortality, organ support free days). APRIL's core biological function is promoting B cell survival and activation, playing a role in humoral immunity.
Sport Implications: The findings are specific to critically ill COVID-19 patients and do not provide information relevant to understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. The study's focus is on disease-state immunology and treatment response, lacking any context applicable to exercise physiology or sports performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The document describes the development and validation of somatic cell genome editing technologies for disease-relevant somatic cells, focusing on the use of viral vectors like AAV for gene delivery in preclinical animal models.
Effect Summary: AAV capsid proteins are examined in vivo as endogenous CEST MRI contrast mechanisms. Higher levels of these proteins indicate the successful delivery and transduction of gene-editing cargo, allowing for non-invasive tracking of the therapeutic agent's distribution and efficacy.
Sport Implications: The findings pertain to the tracking of gene-editing cargo delivery for therapeutic applications in the context of disease treatment. There is no information provided to suggest a direct link between AAV capsid protein levels and an athlete's training stress, physiological adaptation, performance, or recovery processes. Therefore, this biomarker, as presented, does not offer insights relevant to sports science or exercise physiology.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated early brain injury and cognitive impairment following aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) in patients (WFNS 1 and 2) and used extended genetic-imaging analysis in UK Biobank participants.
Effect Summary: The rs2199936 genetic variant within an exon of ABCG2 was associated with cerebellar lobule VII volume. This variant is also part of many additional variants principally related to cardiovascular disease and risk factors.
Sport Implications: The study primarily investigates early brain injury and cognitive impairment in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage patients and general UK Biobank participants. It has no direct athletic context, population, or intervention related to exercise, training, recovery, or performance. Therefore, these findings do not directly support an interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. While the ABCG2 genetic variant is associated with cardiovascular disease and risk factors, which are general health considerations for athletes, this study does not provide insights into how this genetic variant influences these factors within an athletic population or impacts exercise-specific physiological adaptations.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study focuses on pediatric Philadelphia-negative B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) patients with kinase fusions.
Effect Summary: ABL1 rearrangements were identified in a subset of pediatric B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) patients. These rearrangements are considered oncogenic drivers that promote uncontrolled cell proliferation and survival, and their presence is associated with an inferior prognosis in affected individuals.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are strictly within the context of pediatric oncology, specifically related to genetic rearrangements in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia. There is no information or context relating ABL1 rearrangements to training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation and offer no insights from a sports-science perspective.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study investigated cognitive biomarkers in patients who had experienced aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH), comparing cognitively impaired patients to non-impaired patients at 3 months post-SAH. The study was observational with no specific therapeutic interventions.
Effect Summary: Cognitively impaired patients 3 months post-Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) exhibited significantly lower ACE-R scores (89 ± 5) compared to non-impaired patients (93 ± 5).
Sport Implications: The findings of this study do not support an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery, as it focuses on cognitive impairment following aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage in a non-athletic patient population. While cognitive function is essential for athletic performance, this specific biomarker application in a medical context offers no direct insight into exercise physiology or sports performance parameters.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study investigated molecular signatures in pediatric patients with COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C), comparing disease states and recovery trajectories.
Effect Summary: ADAMTS2 gene transcripts were found to be elevated in the post-acute stage of both Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) and COVID-19. In MIS-C patients, these elevated levels returned to baseline approximately one month post-hospitalization. However, in COVID-19 patients, ADAMTS2 levels remained elevated at the one-month post-hospitalization mark, indicating a more persistent expression in this condition.
Sport Implications: The provided data is derived from a longitudinal observational study in pediatric patients with COVID-19 and MIS-C, characterizing disease states and recovery. There is no athletic context, nor any information linking ADAMTS2 expression or its role in extracellular matrix remodeling to training load, recovery, adaptation, performance, or overtraining in athletes. Therefore, no sport-specific implications can be drawn from these findings.

Activity Context Summary: The study focuses on developing and validating predictive models for cognitive impairment and dementia in general adult populations (age 40-75, >60 years) using epigenetic markers and CSF biomarkers. No athlete population, exercise intervention, or specific training state is reported.
Effect Summary: The ADAS-Q4 cognitive assessment score was significantly associated (FDR-adjusted P = 0.03) in the anticipated direction with a Multivariate Methylation Risk Score (MMRS-MCI) at baseline in a cohort studying cognitive impairment and dementia, underscoring the model's robustness in capturing cognitive variations.
Sport Implications: This biomarker, used as a cognitive assessment for dementia in non-athletic, general populations, provides no direct insights into training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. The findings do NOT support athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: This biomarker is evaluated within the context of nutrigenetics and personalized sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes. The interventions include various nutritional approaches and specifically caffeine supplementation, with athletes engaging in diverse exercise regimens such as cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, and exercise under heat stress.
Effect Summary: The ADORA2A rs5751876 SNP categorizes individuals into 'high' (TT genotype) or 'low' (CT or CC genotypes) caffeine sensitivity due to its role in adenosine receptor modulation. However, the findings indicate that this specific SNP had no observable effect on either cognitive performance or exercise performance in response to caffeine supplementation.
Sport Implications: This biomarker helps predict an athlete's individual caffeine sensitivity, which could inform personalized caffeine intake strategies to manage subjective responses. However, the findings explicitly state that for this specific SNP, there was no observed impact on exercise or cognitive performance following caffeine supplementation. Therefore, while it provides insight into individual variability in caffeine response, its utility for directly optimizing athletic performance (training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery) through caffeine appears limited based on the current evidence for this SNP.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study focused on biomarker discovery and characterization for Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy (SBMA) in human patients and AR113Q mouse models. Samples were collected from adult male SBMA patients and age-matched healthy controls, and gene expression was analyzed in skeletal muscle from androgen receptor knockout (Ar-KO) mice after DHT administration.
Effect Summary: ADP-Ribosyltransferase 3 (ART3) protein levels were observed to be lower in the plasma of adult male patients with Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy (SBMA). This decrease in plasma ART3 protein significantly correlated with a higher thigh MRI muscle fat fraction. Additionally, ART3 gene expression was found to be downregulated in skeletal muscle from Ar-KO mice following dihydrotestosterone (DHT) administration.
Sport Implications: The provided findings do not support an athletic interpretation. The research exclusively investigates ART3 in the context of Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy (SBMA), a specific neurodegenerative disease, and its correlation with disease-specific muscle pathology (e.g., muscle fat infiltration in SBMA patients). There is no information regarding ART3's role in response to exercise, training stress, recovery, adaptation, performance, muscle damage and repair processes, or physiological changes in healthy athletic populations.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The findings are derived from adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) patients undergoing chemotherapy and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
Effect Summary: AFDN wild-type gene transcript expression in bone marrow samples was observed to increase by 2-fold during Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) relapse compared to initial diagnosis. Following (7+3) induction chemotherapy and HIDAC consolidation in an AML patient, its expression significantly decreased by 5.5-fold.
Sport Implications: The presented findings are entirely within a clinical context focused on Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) pathology and treatment response. There is no athletic context, information on exercise interventions, training states, or performance outcomes. Therefore, these findings do not support any interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study introduces a computational algorithm (MiSL) for identifying mutation-specific synthetic lethal partners and predictive genetic biomarkers in cancer. The context involves pan-cancer human primary tumor data, various cancer types (e.g., breast cancer), and therapeutic interventions (gene knockdown, pharmacological inhibition) in cancer cell lines and animal models for precision oncology.
Effect Summary: AKT1, a key protein in cell signaling pathways regulating cell growth, proliferation, and survival, was investigated in the context of cancer. Findings showed that AKT1 deletion resulted in lowered expression. AKT1 deletion and PIK3CA mutation were found to be mutually exclusive in pan-cancer data. Conversely, AKT1 was overexpressed in PIK3CA-mutant breast cancer. AKT1 was identified as a target for the therapeutic inhibitor MK-2206, particularly in breast cancer with PIK3CA mutation, where it forms a synthetic lethal interaction.
Sport Implications: The findings are exclusively related to cancer research, focusing on identifying predictive biomarkers and therapeutic targets for cancer treatment. There is no information provided that supports an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This was a case-control observational study investigating plasma levels of 16 trace elements and 27 AMD-associated genetic variants in 236 individuals with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) and 236 age-matched controls.
Effect Summary: Various AMD-associated genetic variants (e.g., CFH (rs10922109), ARMS2/HTRA1 (rs3750846)) showed no statistically significant association with plasma trace element levels or nAMD status in the studied cohort.
Sport Implications: This study investigates genetic variants associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and their relationship with trace element levels in a general population. The findings lack any athletic context, as the study population consists of individuals with nAMD and age-matched controls, without any mention of training, exercise, or athletic performance. Therefore, this biomarker and its observed effects, as reported in this study, do not provide information relevant to understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: The study involved female Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) patients and healthy controls performing two maximal incremental cycle ergometer tests 24 hours apart. However, the specific finding for AMPK phosphorylation was observed in muscle cells (in vitro) from these ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, stimulated with electric pulses. No athlete or specific exercise training context for AMPK phosphorylation measurement was reported.
Effect Summary: In vitro electric pulse stimulation of muscle cells derived from ME/CFS patients showed impaired AMPK phosphorylation compared to muscle cells from healthy individuals.
Sport Implications: The findings are derived from a clinical population (ME/CFS patients) and conducted in an in vitro setting using muscle cells, rather than directly from athletes undergoing training or competition. While AMP-activated Protein Kinase (AMPK) is a critical regulator of cellular energy homeostasis and plays a key role in metabolic adaptations to exercise, this specific study does not provide direct insights into training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in healthy athletes. High-intensity Interval Training (HIIT) evoked larger reductions in motor threshold compared to Moderate-intensity Continuous Training (MICT). These changes were associated with recovery improvements post-stroke.
Sport Implications: The findings are derived from a population of post-stroke individuals undergoing rehabilitation, not healthy athletes. Therefore, this biomarker's response to exercise in this context does not directly provide insights into training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in an athletic population. The study has no athletic context.

Biomarker: Active Muscle Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE-AM)
Activity Context Summary: This study involved resistance-trained males participating in a resistance exercise protocol consisting of full squat sets (3x8 repetitions at 70% 1RM, velocity-based). The intervention included oral phenylcapsaicin (PC) supplementation (low dose 0.625 mg, high dose 2.5 mg) or placebo, administered 45 minutes before exercise. RPE-AM was assessed immediately after each set.
Effect Summary: High-dose phenylcapsaicin (2.5 mg) supplementation resulted in significantly lower Active Muscle Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE-AM) during full squat exercise compared to both a low dose (0.625 mg) and a placebo. This indicates a reduced localized perceived exertion associated with the active muscles.
Sport Implications: RPE-AM serves as a valuable tool for monitoring internal training load, reflecting the subjective effort experienced by specific active muscles during exercise. A reduction in RPE-AM for a given external load, as observed with high-dose phenylcapsaicin, suggests anti-fatigue effects and potentially enhanced exercise tolerance. This could allow athletes to sustain higher training volumes or intensities before reaching subjective fatigue limits, thereby potentially amplifying adaptive stimuli. This biomarker directly aids in understanding acute training stress and can inform strategies to modulate perceived effort, which is critical for optimizing performance and programming training loads.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated metabolic reprogramming in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients treated with Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor.
Effect Summary: After 7 days of sorafenib treatment, acyl-carnitine ratios (Acetyl-carnitine (C2) to free carnitine (C0) ratio, and C2 + propionyl-carnitine (C3) to C0 ratio) were reduced. Total levels of short and medium acyl-carnitines were also reduced, which confirms impaired fatty acid oxidation under sorafenib treatment.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are derived from a study on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and the effects of sorafenib treatment, with no reported athletic context, intervention, or population. Therefore, these specific findings do not support an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery.

Biomarker: Adaptive Immunity Pathway and Antigen Presentation
Activity Context Summary: This study involved 25 healthy female physique athletes undergoing a prolonged intensive physical training regimen combined with a severe energy-restricted diet for 21.1 weeks (resulting in ~29% decreased energy availability and substantial fat mass loss), followed by an 18.4-week weight regain period with reduced exercise and increased energy intake.
Effect Summary: During the intense weight loss period, there was significant downregulation of the adaptive immunity pathway, Class I MHC mediated antigen processing and presentation, and antigen pathway associated with ubiquitination and proteasome degradation in leukocytes. Accompanying these changes were dysregulated hematopoiesis, suppressed immune cell proliferation (T- and B-lymphocytes), attenuated systemic inflammation, reduced antibody-mediated function (decreased total IgG levels and altered IgG glycosylation towards pro-inflammatory activity with reduced affinity), and suppressed IgE-dependent immune reactions, as well as suppressed cytotoxic CD8 T-lymphocyte lineage fate. Most of these immune system parameters largely reverted to baseline during the subsequent weight regain period.
Sport Implications: The significant downregulation of adaptive immunity pathways and widespread immunosuppression observed in female physique athletes under conditions of prolonged intensive training and low energy availability indicates a state of severe physiological stress and underrecovery. This compromised immune function could increase susceptibility to infections, leading to illness and disrupted training continuity, thereby negatively impacting performance. The suppressed T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation and reduced antibody function suggest an impaired capacity for immune surveillance and pathogen defense. Reversal of these immune alterations during the weight regain period highlights the critical role of adequate energy availability and appropriate training load in maintaining immune health and facilitating recovery and adaptation in athletes. While 'attenuated systemic inflammation' was noted, it is within a context of overall immune suppression, suggesting a blunted rather than a healthy inflammatory response capacity, which can hinder appropriate tissue repair and adaptation.

Activity Context Summary: This study involved both untrained and resistance-trained male participants undergoing an 8-week progressive high-intensity resistance training program (3 times/week). The intervention included daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation.
Effect Summary: Cistanche deserticola supplementation was associated with elevated and facilitated rapid supply of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP). Although specific quantification in human data was not provided, this effect is based on mechanistic understanding derived from the study's overall findings.
Sport Implications: ATP is the fundamental energy currency for muscular contraction and all cellular processes related to exercise. Enhanced ATP availability and a more rapid supply capacity, as suggested by these findings, directly supports sustained physical performance, delays exercise-induced fatigue, and improves muscle strength. This has significant implications for training adaptation by potentially allowing for higher training volumes or intensities, and for recovery by ensuring adequate energy for cellular repair and regeneration. Monitoring factors influencing ATP supply can help in understanding an athlete's capacity for performance, fatigue resistance, and overall energy status for adaptation.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study involves a proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) against their somatic origins.
Effect Summary: Adenylate Kinase 3 (AK3) protein expression was observed to be lower (down-regulated) in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) compared to human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
Sport Implications: The findings describe specific proteomic differences related to energy metabolism between various stem cell lines (hiPSCs and hESCs). As there is no athletic or exercise context reported in this study, these findings do not provide direct insights into training stress, adaptation, performance, recovery, or any other aspect of sports medicine and exercise physiology in athletes. Therefore, no sports-specific implications can be drawn from this data.

Activity Context Summary: The provided findings describe the proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) against their parental somatic cells, specifically reporting on AT1B3 (CD298) and not Adhesion G Protein-Coupled Receptor E2 (ADGRE2). This study lacks any athletic or exercise context; therefore, no information regarding ADGRE2's activity in athletes or its relation to training state, intervention, or recovery can be inferred from this data.
Effect Summary: The provided data reports on AT1B3 (CD298), a subunit of Na+/K+-ATPase, noting its involvement in ion transport and cell signaling. Protein levels of AT1B3 were observed to be higher (at least 1.5-fold) in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) compared to their parental somatic cells. This observation was made in the context of identifying potential pluripotency markers for stem cells.
