The substantial increase in blood IL-10 after an ultramarathon highlights its critical role in the anti-inflammatory response to extreme exercise, aiding in the mitigation of muscle damage and systemic inflammation, thereby supporting recovery and adaptation processes. Monitoring IL-10 levels could assist coaches and sports scientists in assessing the inflammatory burden, recovery status, and the effectiveness of training interventions. This allows for fine-tuning training loads to optimize adaptation, maintain physiological homeostasis, and potentially prevent underrecovery or overtraining. The findings from Yogic Breathing did not demonstrate a significant acute impact on salivary IL-10, suggesting that a single short session might not elicit a measurable inflammatory response or that salivary IL-10 may not be the most sensitive marker for such interventions in healthy individuals. Findings from disease contexts lack direct athletic applicability.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The studies investigated Interleukin 12 (IL-12) in various non-athletic contexts including: an in vitro osteoarthritic knee joint explant co-culture model, mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapy for COVID-19 associated Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), immune dysregulation in COVID-19 patients with comorbidities, stem cell therapy (MSC and neural stem cells) for neurodegenerative and oncological brain disorders, peripheral immune signatures in chronic Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients, an in vitro human triple-culture air-blood barrier model with differentiated macrophage phenotypes, and biomarker identification for severe dengue disease progression.
Effect Summary: Interleukin 12 (IL-12) displayed varied effects across the reported studies. In an in vitro osteoarthritic joint explant model, IL-12 levels decreased in response to hyperacute serum treatment. Mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) therapy led to decreased production of IL-12 in the context of ARDS. Conversely, high serum levels of IL-12 were observed in severe COVID-19 patients compared to those with uncomplicated SARS. In patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), serum IL-12 was significantly higher compared to control and non-malignant patients, being lowest in chronic HCV patients, but increasing in cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic patients who achieved sustained virologic response (SVR) after direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment. In severe dengue disease with comorbidities, plasma IL-12 levels were lower, with a borderline significant decrease compared to severe dengue without comorbidities. In an in vitro model of differentiated THP-1 cells and triple cultures, IL-12 was undetectable via ELISA. Furthermore, a specific beta glucan supplement did not stimulate IL-12 production in cultured peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and U937 cells. The direction and magnitude of IL-12 change in brain homogenates of Alzheimer's disease mouse models were not specified in the provided text.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are exclusively within the context of disease pathology (e.g., osteoarthritis, COVID-19, ARDS, liver disease, dengue, neurodegenerative disorders) or in vitro experimental models. There is no athletic context, exercise intervention, or healthy athlete population reported across any of the documents. Therefore, these findings do not support any interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This observational study investigated innate immune functions in children with Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome (MIS-C) following SARS-CoV-2 exposure, focusing on in vitro cellular responses to Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonists (LPS stimulation).
Effect Summary: Interleukin 12 Subunit p40 (IL-12p40) protein production and gene expression levels were much lower in response to LPS stimulation in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from children with Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome (MIS-C), both acutely and in convalescence, compared to healthy controls.
Sport Implications: The findings from this study are derived from a population of children with Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome (MIS-C) and lack any athletic or exercise context. Therefore, direct implications for understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes cannot be drawn from this data. The observed immune hyporesponsiveness relates to a specific pathological state rather than adaptations to exercise.

Activity Context Summary: One study involved aerobically trained individuals undergoing a half-marathon run, investigating the effects of short-term Montmorency tart cherry supplementation. Other findings are derived from studies on patients with Behçet’s disease, recurrent aphthous stomatitis, and healthy controls, some of whom were receiving immunosuppressive therapies. Additionally, an in vitro study examined human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) on PBMC cytokine secretion. The latter two contexts are not athletic.
Effect Summary: In the context of a half-marathon run and tart cherry supplementation, the change in serum Interleukin 12 Subunit p70 (IL-12p70) concentration was not reported. In a non-athletic context (Behçet’s disease), salivary IL-12p70 levels were generally lower compared to healthy controls, but increased in recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) saliva. In Behçet’s disease patients, combination immunosuppressive therapy (Colchicine + Azathioprine) significantly lowered salivary IL-12p70 compared to Azathioprine monotherapy. Salivary IL-12p70 also showed positive correlations with IL-5, TNF-β, and IL-10 in Behçet’s disease patients. Serum IL-12p70 levels remained unchanged in Behçet’s disease patients relative to healthy controls. In an in vitro setting, IL-12p70 secretion from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) was remarkably attenuated when co-cultured with UC-MSC.
Sport Implications: While IL-12p70 is a key pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in immune responses, the provided data offers limited direct insights into its role in athletic training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery. In the only study featuring an athletic population and intervention (half-marathon, tart cherry supplementation), IL-12p70 levels were not reported. The remaining findings stem from disease-specific contexts (Behçet’s disease, COVID-19) and thus do not allow for sport-specific interpretation regarding training, recovery, or performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported.
Effect Summary: IL-13 protein levels were observed to be higher in an in vitro osteoarthritic knee joint explant co-culture model when stimulated with the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β, signifying an anti-inflammatory response. Conversely, IL-13 plasma concentrations were found to be lower in acute dengue patients, showing an altered immune response during infection, and directly correlated with other cytokines (MIP-1α, IL-1β, IL-7) and platelet counts.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are derived from an in vitro model of osteoarthritis and an observational study on patients with dengue infection. Neither context involves athletes, exercise, training states, or performance-related interventions. Consequently, these specific findings do not directly offer insights into understanding training stress, adaptation, athletic performance, or recovery in athletes. While IL-13 is recognized as an anti-inflammatory cytokine, these studies do not provide data on its role in exercise-induced inflammation, muscle damage and repair processes, or cardiovascular/endocrine adaptations to training.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated IL-15 response in healthy male volunteers undergoing resistance exercise to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and the effect of NPN_1 supplementation on recovery. Two other studies lack an athletic context: one was an observational study on adult dengue patients, and the other investigated biomarkers for aging and cellular senescence in healthy human participants.
Effect Summary: IL-15 plasma levels were elevated (p=0.159) following NPN_1 supplementation, with a significantly higher release immediately post-DOMS compared to baseline within the NPN_1 group, returning to baseline within 2 hours post-exercise. In non-athletic contexts, IL-15 was found to be higher in acute dengue infection compared to healthy subjects, particularly in severe cases, and correlated with other inflammatory cytokines. Additionally, serum IL-15 was positively correlated with increasing chronological age.
Sport Implications: As a myokine, the elevation of IL-15 immediately following resistance exercise-induced muscle damage suggests a role in muscle anabolism, repair, and regeneration processes. Its association with promoting muscle growth and anti-catabolic effects indicates that IL-15 could be a valuable marker for monitoring muscle recovery and adaptation to training stress. The early post-exercise increase may reflect the initiation of reparative responses, potentially contributing to improved strength recovery and reduced fatigue, especially when modulated by nutritional interventions. The findings from dengue infection and aging are not directly applicable to understanding training stress or adaptation in healthy athletes.

Activity Context Summary:
In an athletic context, Interleukin 17A (IL-17A) levels were observed in young male soccer players (aged 13.0 ± 0.2 years) undergoing regular sports activity and pre-seasonal training, where it was analyzed for its predictive ability on fitness parameters. IL-17A was also studied in elite male badminton and soccer players, comparing their blood plasma levels during 'recovered' (after rest) versus 'non-recovered' (after habitual loading microcycles involving intensive, sport-specific training) states. 

No athlete or exercise context was reported for studies involving healthy volunteers undergoing Yogic Breathing, in vitro osteoarthritic knee joint explant models, COVID-19 patients, lung transplant patients, dengue patients, Adult-onset Still's disease patients, Behçet’s disease/recurrent aphthous stomatitis patients, or individuals with neuroinflammatory conditions or generalized anxiety disorder.
Effect Summary:
In athletic populations, blood plasma IL-17A levels were significantly higher in elite badminton and soccer players when in a non-recovered state following habitual loading microcycles compared to a recovered state (e.g., badminton players: 48.5 ± 25.2 pg/mL in non-recovered vs. 38.7 ± 11.4 pg/mL in recovered, p = 0.018). Lower blood IL-17A levels were negatively associated with better Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance in young male soccer players, suggesting lower levels are predictive of better explosive jump ability. 

In non-athletic contexts, salivary IL-17A was unchanged after a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing session in healthy volunteers. IL-17A levels decreased in an in vitro osteoarthritic joint model with hyperacute serum treatment. Systemic IL-17 reduction was targeted to reduce cardiovascular progression in COVID-19. Plasma IL-17 was lower at 72 hours post-lung transplant in association with severe graft dysfunction. Plasma IL-17A was lower in acute dengue patients compared to healthy subjects. Salivary IL-17A showed a small, non-significant increase in Behçet’s disease patients, while serum detection was often difficult. Serum IL-17A was found to be higher in generalized anxiety disorder patients. No specific results were available from studies involving clarithromycin treatment for COVID-19 or neuroinflammatory conditions, as these were study protocols.
Sport Implications:
Interleukin 17A (IL-17A) demonstrates potential utility in sports science for monitoring training load, recovery, and performance readiness. The observed elevation of blood plasma IL-17A in elite athletes during non-recovered states following habitual training indicates its value as a biomarker for systemic inflammatory response to exercise stress. Regular monitoring could help identify periods of cumulative fatigue and potentially inadequate recovery, guiding individualized training adjustments to prevent overtraining.

Furthermore, the negative association between blood IL-17A and Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance in young soccer players suggests that lower levels of inflammation are linked to superior explosive power. This positions IL-17A as a potential diagnostic indicator for an athlete's physiological state and capacity for high-intensity performance. A decrease in IL-17A levels during recovery periods would signify effective management of exercise-induced inflammation and successful adaptation, supporting overall athlete well-being and performance optimization.

Activity Context Summary: The provided studies investigate Interleukin 18 (IL-18) in various clinical populations including patients with septic shock caused by multidrug-resistant bacteria, adult dengue patients categorized by disease severity (mild vs. severe, with/without comorbidities), patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) and cellular therapies, and in the context of acute and chronic respiratory diseases such as ARDS, COVID-19, and COPD. No athlete or exercise context reported.
Effect Summary: Interleukin 18 (IL-18) consistently shows elevated levels across several severe inflammatory and disease states. In septic shock patients, IL-18 gene transcript expression in CD14+ monocytes showed a marked tendency to increase. Plasma IL-18 protein levels were significantly increased in all dengue cases compared to healthy subjects, with particularly high levels observed during the acute febrile phase and in severe dengue disease, especially when accompanied by comorbidities. These elevated levels were positively associated with other inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TNF-α, VEGF, IL-1Rα) and negatively correlated with platelet counts. IL-18 protein levels in blood/serum are also associated with predictive or diagnostic value for acute Graft-versus-Host Disease (aGVHD) post-transplant, and its levels are reported to increase in lung injury conditions such as ARDS, COVID-19, and COPD, where it contributes to increased vascular permeability and tissue damage.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are derived exclusively from studies on severe disease states and pathological conditions (septic shock, dengue, post-transplant complications, and respiratory diseases). These contexts do not involve healthy individuals undergoing exercise or training, nor do they explore the physiological responses to athletic endeavors. Therefore, these specific findings do not directly support an interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The studies investigated IL-18BP in the context of Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) pathogenesis, post-allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (TCT) for immune monitoring and acute Graft-versus-Host Disease (aGVHD) prediction, and its secretion by prostate cancer cells.
Effect Summary: IL-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) is an intrinsic inhibitor of Interleukin-18 (IL-18), neutralizing its proinflammatory activity and inhibiting IL-18-mediated NF-κB activation and proinflammatory cytokine production. Decreased levels of IL-18BP (both protein and mRNA) were observed in active Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) patients, after Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) ligand treatment, and with microRNA-134 (miR-134) overexpression, leading to elevated free IL-18 levels and contributing to inflammation. IL-18BP levels in blood/serum have been associated with predictive or diagnostic value for acute Graft-versus-Host Disease (aGVHD). Elevated secretion of IL-18BP by prostate cancer cells has also been noted, suggested to be an effort by these cells to modulate immune responses.
Sport Implications: The provided studies do not directly involve athletes or exercise. Therefore, no direct sports-specific implications can be drawn from these findings. However, given that IL-18BP is a key modulator of IL-18-driven inflammation, and inflammation is a critical component of exercise-induced adaptation, recovery from training stress, and potential under-recovery/overtraining, IL-18BP could theoretically be a relevant biomarker in sports science. If its levels were found to reflect systemic inflammatory load related to IL-18 in athletes, monitoring IL-18BP might offer insights into inflammatory status, recovery efficiency, and adaptive responses to training. For example, persistently low IL-18BP could indicate an unmitigated IL-18 inflammatory response, potentially signaling excessive training stress or insufficient recovery, which could impede performance and increase the risk of overtraining. However, this is purely speculative based on its biological function, as no athletic data is presented here.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated the IL-18 rs1946518 polymorphism and other biomarkers in patients with breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers, and myocardial infarction, compared to healthy controls, as part of a diagnostic biomarker and genetic polymorphism study.
Effect Summary: The IL-18 rs1946518 polymorphism (-607 C/A) showed varied associations with disease risk: the AA genotype and A allele were significantly associated with an increased risk for Prostate Cancer (PCa). For Colorectal Cancer (CRC), A/C heterozygotes showed an increased risk, while C allele homozygotes were protected. For Breast Cancer (BC), conflicting findings were reported, with one suggesting no significant association and another indicating an Odds Ratio of 1.75 for both C and A alleles as a risk factor. This genetic variation is understood to affect IL-18 gene transcription, influencing immune response and disease susceptibility.
Sport Implications: These findings are exclusively derived from a study on disease susceptibility in clinical populations (cancer and myocardial infarction patients vs. healthy controls). There is no information provided within the study that relates this polymorphism to athletic performance, training stress, recovery, adaptation, or any other aspect of sports science. Therefore, the findings do not support an athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated advanced chronic heart failure patients undergoing Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD) support, comparing baseline inflammatory markers between responders and non-responders to the intervention.
Effect Summary: In advanced heart failure patients, lower baseline circulating (serum) Interleukin (IL)-5 levels were significantly associated with better cardiac structural and functional improvement following durable LVAD support. IL-5 was also detected in myocardial tissue of failing human hearts, though at relatively lower levels compared to other inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, IL-7, IL-13), and myocardial tissue levels of IL-5 did not significantly differ between responders and non-responders to LVAD therapy.
Sport Implications: These findings are derived from a clinical population with advanced heart failure undergoing mechanical circulatory support (LVAD) and do not provide direct insight into training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in healthy athletes. The observed association between lower IL-5 and cardiac improvement in this disease context is not transferable to athletic performance or training parameters.

Activity Context Summary: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) levels were monitored in endurance-trained female runners following a single bout of strenuous downhill running, with and without multi-ingredient performance supplement (MIPS) pre-loading. It was also assessed in endurance athletes after high-intensity continuous endurance running field tests and during subsequent recovery phases. Elite male athletes (badminton and soccer players) were studied to compare IL-6 levels in 'recovered' versus 'non-recovered' states following habitual loading microcycles involving intensive, sport-specific training. Furthermore, its response was examined in professional volleyball players after submaximal physical exercise, both with and without whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) intervention, and in rowers after an exhaustive 2000-m rowing ergometer test, with and without cranberry extract supplementation. Two studies investigated IL-6 in non-athletic contexts: advanced heart failure patients undergoing Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD) support, and COVID-19 patients.
Effect Summary: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) consistently increases immediately after various forms of strenuous exercise, including downhill running (peaking with a 62.99% increase), high-intensity continuous endurance running, and exhaustive rowing. These elevated levels can persist for several hours (up to 72 hours post-DHR) or normalize within 24 hours. IL-6 levels are generally higher in elite athletes during 'non-recovered' states following habitual loading microcycles compared to 'recovered' states (e.g., mean difference of 1.3 pg/mL overall, 1.9 pg/mL in soccer players). Whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) administered before exercise has been shown to result in lower exercise-induced IL-6 levels compared to control exercise without WBC. Neither multi-ingredient performance supplements (MIPS) nor cranberry extract supplementation significantly modulated the exercise-induced IL-6 response in the studies reviewed. In non-athletic contexts, lower circulating IL-6 levels were observed in advanced heart failure patients showing cardiac improvement after LVAD support, while higher levels were found in COVID-19 patients with specific lipid profiles.
Sport Implications: Interleukin 6 (IL-6) serves as a robust indicator of acute physiological stress and inflammatory response following various types of strenuous exercise, including eccentric (downhill running) and exhaustive endurance activities (running, rowing). Its elevation reflects muscle damage, the initiation of immune responses, and the need for recovery processes such as glycogen replenishment and muscle repair. Elevated IL-6 levels in 'non-recovered' states, particularly after habitual heavy training microcycles, suggest its utility in monitoring training load and identifying potential under-recovery, thereby potentially informing training adjustments to prevent overtraining. Whole-body cryotherapy appears to attenuate exercise-induced IL-6 levels, indicating a potential role in modulating inflammatory recovery. However, the moderate reliability of IL-6 measurements in some athletic contexts suggests that while it reflects general exercise response, its precision for individual monitoring of training load and recovery might be limited compared to more reliable markers. The studies involving advanced heart failure patients and COVID-19 patients have no athletic context and thus do not support athletic interpretation regarding training, recovery, or performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigates advanced heart failure patients undergoing Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD) support, focusing on baseline inflammatory markers as predictors for cardiac structural and functional improvement post-intervention.
Effect Summary: In advanced heart failure patients undergoing LVAD support, lower baseline circulating levels of Interleukin (IL)-7 were significantly associated with better cardiac structural and functional improvement. Higher serum levels were linked to negatively affecting this improvement. Myocardial levels of IL-7 were detected but showed no significant difference between patients who responded well to LVAD support and those who did not.
Sport Implications: This study's findings are based on a population of advanced heart failure patients undergoing a medical intervention (LVAD support). This context is entirely unrelated to healthy athletic populations, exercise training, recovery, or performance adaptation. Therefore, the findings do not directly support an athletic interpretation or provide insights into training stress, recovery, or performance in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated the response of Interleukin 8 (IL-8) in endurance athletes performing two identical 60-minute continuous endurance running field tests, designed to induce exhaustion (40 minutes at 95% HR at Individual Anaerobic Threshold (IAT) followed by 20 minutes at 110% HR at IAT). Another study involved healthy volunteers undergoing a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing session. A third study examined IL-8 levels in advanced heart failure patients receiving durable Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD) support; this context is not directly athletic.
Effect Summary: Salivary IL-8 significantly reduced (3–6 orders lower than control) immediately and up to 20 minutes after a single 20-minute Yogic Breathing session in healthy volunteers. In endurance athletes, blood IL-8 increased immediately after 60-minute strenuous endurance running bouts, then decreased 3 hours post-exercise, demonstrating moderate reliability (ICC = 0.67). In a non-athletic context, serum IL-8 levels were unchanged in advanced heart failure patients undergoing LVAD support, and myocardial levels were detected at lower levels compared to other cytokines in the failing heart.
Sport Implications: In an athletic context, the acute elevation of blood Interleukin 8 (IL-8) immediately following strenuous endurance exercise signifies its role in the body's acute inflammatory response to high training stress. The subsequent decrease 3 hours post-exercise suggests its involvement in the early phase of recovery from this acute inflammatory process. However, the reported moderate reliability (ICC = 0.67) for monitoring exercise response suggests that IL-8 might have limitations as a standalone marker for consistently tracking individual training load and recovery status over time in athletes. While not directly studied in athletes, the observed reduction of salivary IL-8 following Yogic Breathing in healthy volunteers could speculatively suggest a potential non-pharmacological strategy for managing exercise-induced inflammatory responses or stress in athletes if such practices were incorporated into recovery protocols. The findings from advanced heart failure patients provide no athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: The study investigated 75 middle-aged adults undergoing acute symptom-limited treadmill exercise (following a standard Bruce protocol) and a 20-week aerobic exercise training program (three sessions per week, with intensity and duration gradually increased). The population is not defined as athletes, and the acute exercise was a stress test rather than a performance-oriented training session.
Effect Summary: Plasma levels of interleukin proteins and their receptors were observed to change at peak acute exercise. The specific numerical magnitude of change was not quantified, but the direction of change was noted to be similar to previous findings.
Sport Implications: While interleukin proteins are critical components of the immune and inflammatory response to exercise, playing roles in recovery, adaptation, and muscle repair, the findings here are derived from a study involving middle-aged adults undergoing a diagnostic stress test and general aerobic training. This context limits direct application to specific athletic training load monitoring, performance diagnostics, or tailored recovery strategies for competitive athletes. The study confirms that these biomarkers are responsive to acute exercise, but it does not offer specific insights into overtraining, underrecovery, or performance in a high-performance athletic population.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients, without an athletic context. The other study involved endurance athletes performing two identical 60-minute continuous endurance running field tests (RFTs) at high intensity (40 min at 95% HR at Individual Anaerobic Threshold, followed by 20 min at 110% HR at IAT) to ensure exhaustion. This was conducted to monitor exercise response and recovery processes.
Effect Summary: In FIRES patients, IL1RA activity in CSF was observed to be higher (restored/robustly suppressed) after Anakinra therapy, indicating effective restoration of IL1R signaling inhibition. In endurance athletes, blood plasma IL-1RA concentration increased immediately after a 60-minute high-intensity endurance running test, peaked 3 hours post-exercise, and returned to baseline within 24 hours. This biomarker demonstrated moderate to excellent reliability for monitoring and showed significant associations with muscular fatigue indicators (MVC knee flexors and extensors) immediately after exercise.
Sport Implications: The increase in IL-1RA following strenuous endurance exercise and its subsequent return to baseline within 24 hours suggests it serves as a responsive physiological marker of acute exercise-induced immune activation and the progression of recovery in athletes. Its reported reliability and suitability indicate its potential utility for monitoring athletes' training load management, providing insights into the immediate post-exercise inflammatory response and recovery status. The observed association with muscular fatigue (MVC) further suggests a link to the physiological stress response impacting muscle function post-exercise. The first study has no athletic context and therefore provides no sport-specific implications.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study investigates genetic variants in patients with Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) and other epilepsy conditions, as well as healthy controls.
Effect Summary: The study identified the presence of noncoding polymorphisms within the IL1RN gene in the DNA of FIRES patients. Specifically, 15 polymorphisms were found between exons 2 and 3, including a TTC duplication at position 2:113121042 and substitutions at 2:113121134 (C to A) and 2:113121138 (A to G). No variants were detected in the translated coding sequences. These intronic mutations are associated with potential splicing changes that could alter IL1RN isoform expression, possibly leading to a functional deficiency of IL1RA.
Sport Implications: This study investigates genetic polymorphisms in the IL1RN gene in the context of Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) and does not provide an athletic or exercise context. Therefore, direct implications for understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes cannot be drawn from these findings. The findings are specific to a neurological disease condition and do not pertain to normal physiological responses to exercise or training.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients, healthy controls, and other epilepsy conditions.
Effect Summary: Interleukin-1 Receptor Antagonist isoform 1 mRNA expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was marginally increased (not statistically significant) in FIRES patients compared to healthy controls. This isoform represented 11.5% of total IL1RN expression in FIRES patient PBMCs, versus approximately 2.5% in healthy control PBMCs. This proportional increase is considered a consequence of a severe reduction in dominant intracellular IL1RN isoforms, rather than an indicator of improved IL1RA function.
Sport Implications: This study's findings are entirely derived from a clinical population with Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) and other neurological conditions, with no reported athletic or exercise context. Therefore, these specific findings regarding IL1RN isoform 1 mRNA expression in PBMCs do not provide information relevant to understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. The observed changes are specific to a severe disease state and cannot be extrapolated to athletic populations.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients, comparing their peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) to those of healthy controls and patients with other epilepsy conditions.
Effect Summary: In peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients, the gene transcript levels of Interleukin-1 Receptor Antagonist isoform 2 mRNA were found to be profoundly lower, present at less than 10% of healthy control levels. This specific isoform is a dominant intracellular IL1RN transcript known to be involved in acute inflammatory responses.
Sport Implications: These findings are exclusively from a study investigating Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES), a neurological disorder, and do not involve any athletic population, exercise intervention, or performance metrics. Therefore, these specific findings on IL1RN isoform 2 mRNA expression do not directly support an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery. While IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA) plays a general role in modulating inflammatory responses that are relevant in athletes, the observed profound decrease in this specific isoform's mRNA in a disease context cannot be extrapolated to exercise physiology or athletic performance without dedicated research in that domain.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study investigates Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients, healthy controls, and individuals with other epilepsy conditions.
Effect Summary: A profound decrease in Interleukin-1 Receptor Antagonist isoform 3 mRNA expression (to <5% of healthy control levels) was observed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients compared to healthy controls. This reduction, along with other factors, contributed to a functional deficiency in IL1RA and impaired IL1R signaling inhibition.
Sport Implications: The findings from this study are exclusively focused on a neurological disorder (Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome) and do not provide direct insights into exercise physiology, training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. The study lacks any athletic or exercise context relevant to sports medicine.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. It does not involve athletic populations, exercise interventions, or training states.
Effect Summary: Interleukin-1 Receptor Antagonist (IL1RN) isoform 4/5 mRNA levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were marginally increased (not statistically significant) in FIRES patients compared to healthy controls. Sport Implications: The findings are derived from a study on Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) and other epilepsy conditions, with no reported athletic context, exercise intervention, or healthy athlete population. Therefore, these specific findings do not provide direct support for understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. The observed changes are in the context of a severe neurological inflammatory condition and cannot be extrapolated to exercise physiology or athletic performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study compares untreated Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients with healthy controls and other epilepsy conditions.
Effect Summary: Total IL1RN mRNA was 21-fold lower in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from untreated Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients compared to healthy controls.
Sport Implications: The findings are derived from a study investigating a specific neurological condition (Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome) and its associated inflammatory dysregulation. Therefore, these specific findings on IL1RN mRNA levels do not directly support an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated IL1R signaling activity in patients with Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) and Epilepsy with Electrical Status Epilepticus during Slow-wave Sleep (ESES), compared to healthy controls and other epilepsy conditions.
Effect Summary: Interleukin-1 Receptor (IL1R) signaling activity was found to be higher in serum from FIRES and ESES patients compared to healthy controls and other epilepsy conditions. Serum from FIRES and ESES patients also demonstrated an exaggerated response to exogenous IL1β and showed resistance to suppression by exogenous IL1RA, unlike samples from healthy controls.
Sport Implications: The findings from this study are derived from a clinical population (epilepsy patients) and lack any athletic context. Therefore, these specific findings do not directly support an athletic interpretation regarding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The findings involve biomarker analysis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients and a study protocol for clarithromycin treatment in mild COVID-19 pneumonia patients.
Effect Summary: In patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), IL1B gene transcript levels were generally higher compared to healthy individuals. Lower co-expression of IL1B with TXNIP and NLRP3 was associated with a more favorable prognosis in AML. Individual IL1B expression alone did not consistently show prognostic significance. For a separate study, the measurement of Interleukin (IL)-1beta cytokine levels in nasal drip is planned for patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia, but no results or observed effects are reported in the provided protocol document.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are entirely within clinical/medical contexts (acute myeloid leukemia prognosis and COVID-19 treatment protocol) and do not contain any information related to athletic populations, training stress, recovery, adaptation, or performance. Therefore, the findings do not support athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated Interleukin-10 (IL-10) responses in endurance athletes undergoing strenuous endurance running field tests and subsequent recovery. Another study examined IL-10 levels in physically active older adults participating in 12 weeks of walking exercise training, with or without daily protein supplementation. The remaining studies focused on women with suspected endometriosis undergoing medical treatment, patients with pulmonary hypertension, and rats with cisplatin-induced kidney injury, none of which provide an athletic or exercise context.
Effect Summary: In women with suspected endometriosis, whole blood IL10 mRNA expression was elevated following elagolix treatment, consistent with its anti-inflammatory roles. Plasma IL10 protein levels were significantly higher in patients with pulmonary hypertension compared to healthy controls, indicating systemic inflammation. Activity Context Summary: IL-6 has been studied in a variety of athletic and exercise contexts including youth soccer training, single bouts of plyometric exercise in adolescent females (obese vs. normal weight), resistance exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), a 160 km ultramarathon, 6 weeks of CrossFit® training (with Tribulus terrestris supplementation), and repeated days of high-intensity simulated road cycling or intermittent sprint activity (with Montmorency cherry concentrate or cocoa flavanol supplementation). It has also been monitored in professional male team sport athletes during intensive training and competition loads, and in physically active older adults participating in a 12-week walking exercise program (with protein supplementation). Additionally, IL-6 has been assessed during inspiratory resistive breathing challenges and in contexts of real-life occupational physical workloads. Some findings relate to spaceflight exposure with in-flight countermeasure training. Many other studies investigate IL-6 in non-athletic, disease-related contexts (e.g., COVID-19, stroke, Heart Failure, Behçet’s disease, dengue, sepsis) or in response to non-exercise interventions (e.g., Yogic Breathing, stem cell therapy, fisetin supplementation), which are not directly relevant to athletic training or performance.
Effect Summary: IL-6 levels generally increase acutely in blood (plasma/serum) following various forms of intense exercise, including plyometric exercise (+31%), ultramarathon running, high-intensity cycling (+65-70%), intermittent sprints, resistance exercise-induced DOMS, and inspiratory resistive breathing. These exercise-induced increases typically return to baseline within minutes to 48 hours. In youth soccer players, higher baseline IL-6 was positively associated with improved performance in explosive vertical jump, aerobic capacity, and repeated sprint ability. In professional team sports, IL-6 elevations were larger and more prolonged after official matches than training, reflecting amplified physiological strain. Supplementation with Montmorency cherry concentrate significantly attenuated exercise-induced IL-6 increases in cyclists and sprinters, while acute cocoa flavanol intake, Tribulus terrestris supplementation during CrossFit, and protein supplementation during walking exercise showed no significant effect on IL-6 levels. Salivary IL-6 often showed no significant changes in response to intense exercise, with values sometimes below detection limits, and its levels can fluctuate diurnally or with acute infections. IL-6 also shows dynamic changes in non-athletic contexts; it can be lowered by MSC therapy, certain nutritional supplements (AFO-202 beta glucan, fisetin), and stem cell treatments in disease models, but is elevated in numerous inflammatory and disease states (e.g., COVID-19, dengue, stroke, Heart Failure, sepsis) and can be suppressed or show complex patterns in specific conditions (e.g., MIS-C, sexual violence recovery). Baseline levels were unaffected by thermal interventions or protein supplementation in active older adults.
Sport Implications: Interleukin-6 is a highly relevant biomarker in sports science, primarily serving as an indicator of acute physiological stress, muscle damage, and inflammatory response to exercise. Its acute elevation post-exercise signals the activation of immune and metabolic pathways important for muscle adaptation and repair. Efficient resolution of this post-exercise IL-6 response, typically by returning to baseline within hours, suggests effective recovery. Conversely, persistently high IL-6 levels, particularly during periods of intense training or congested competition schedules, can signify amplified physiological strain, unresolved inflammation, or insufficient recovery, thus indicating a potential risk for chronic fatigue or overtraining. The positive association between higher baseline IL-6 and improved performance metrics in young athletes suggests that a well-regulated inflammatory signaling (perhaps related to its myokine functions) is integral to adaptation and performance. Interventions like Montmorency cherry concentrate that attenuate exercise-induced IL-6 rises might aid recovery by mitigating excessive inflammatory responses. However, salivary IL-6 appears less reliable for monitoring exercise-induced changes due to low detectability and high variability. Due to its pleiotropic nature and high interindividual variability, IL-6 interpretation requires individual baselines and contextual assessment in conjunction with other markers to effectively guide training load, optimize adaptation, and minimize overtraining and injury risks. The numerous non-athletic findings highlight IL-6's general role in inflammation but do not directly impact its interpretation within a sports and exercise context.

Effect Summary: In patients with cardiac arrhythmias, a 6-week dietary intervention with a specific micronutrient combination showed a tendency for a decrease in interventricular septal thickness (p = 0.053, ES = 0.348). This was associated with a trend towards reduced septal hypertrophy and improved left ventricular diastolic function and cardiometabolic health.
Sport Implications: The findings presented are from a study conducted on patients with cardiac arrhythmias, cardiovascular disorders, and metabolic syndrome, not healthy athletes. Therefore, these specific findings, indicating a beneficial *decrease* in interventricular septal thickness in this clinical population, do not directly translate to understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletic contexts. While interventricular septal thickness is a key measure in sports cardiology to assess physiological cardiac adaptation (athlete's heart) or screen for pathological conditions, the observed effect in this non-athletic, diseased population does not provide direct actionable insights for sports-specific training or performance optimization in healthy individuals.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated Intestinal Fatty Acid Binding Protein (I-FABP) in a cohort of ART-treated men living with HIV, without an athletic context. Another investigation, a scoping review, focused on I-FABP as a serum marker in endurance athletes, particularly during diverse exercise regimens such as cycling, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, and exercise under heat stress. This was often in the context of various nutritional interventions like polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, and probiotics.
Effect Summary: In ART-treated men living with HIV, plasma I-FABP levels remained unchanged and were not associated with performance-based or self-reported cognitive difficulties. In contrast, for endurance athletes, I-FABP serum levels are indicated to be higher post-exercise, especially after prolonged exercise under heat stress, signifying intestinal epithelial injury and increased permeability.
Sport Implications: I-FABP emerges as a relevant biomarker for monitoring acute intestinal epithelial damage and increased gut permeability in endurance athletes, particularly during high physiological stress events like prolonged exercise and heat exposure. Elevated I-FABP levels suggest a compromised gut barrier function, which could have implications for nutrient absorption, contribute to systemic inflammation, and potentially impair recovery and overall performance. Therefore, I-FABP could be a useful tool for assessing training stress, informing recovery strategies, and adjusting training loads to mitigate gut-related issues in athletes. The findings from the non-athletic cohort (ART-treated men living with HIV) are not directly applicable to sports-specific training, recovery, or performance assessment.

Activity Context Summary: This scoping review focuses on endurance athletes undergoing various exercise regimens, including cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, and exercise under heat stress. Specific contexts include prolonged exercise under heat stress, with or without nutritional interventions like cocoa flavanols or low/high FODMAP diets.
Effect Summary: Intestinal permeability generally increases in response to exercise, particularly after prolonged exercise under heat stress. However, specific nutritional interventions, such as cocoa flavanols or low/high FODMAP diets, did not show a significant effect in changing or mitigating these exercise-induced increases.
Sport Implications: Increased intestinal permeability post-exercise, especially in endurance athletes under prolonged or heat stress conditions, serves as an indicator of significant physiological stress. This elevation is linked to potential systemic inflammation or immune activation, which can impact an athlete's recovery processes and overall adaptive responses to training. While observed as a consequence of strenuous exercise, current evidence suggests that interventions like cocoa flavanols or FODMAP diets may not be effective in mitigating this exercise-induced increase. Monitoring this biomarker could offer insights into the acute physiological burden of training and potentially identify athletes at risk of under-recovery or heightened inflammatory states.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated distinct host responses, cellular injury, and tissue damage in pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C).
Effect Summary: Intestinal secretory cell-derived cfRNA levels were significantly higher in plasma samples from patients with Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) compared to controls, indicating intestinal damage or active processes.
Sport Implications: The provided research focuses exclusively on a pediatric clinical population (COVID-19 and MIS-C) and does not involve any athletic participants, exercise interventions, or training contexts. Therefore, these findings do not offer direct insights into understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. Any implications for sports performance, training load monitoring, or recovery would be purely speculative and not supported by the presented data.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigates functional deficiency of endogenous interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL1RA) in Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients, comparing peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from FIRES patients to healthy controls.
Effect Summary: Intracellular IL1RA protein levels were significantly reduced in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of FIRES patients compared to healthy controls. This corresponded to a 21-fold decrease in total IL1RN mRNA levels, indicating reduced expression of intracellular IL1RA isoforms.
Sport Implications: The findings are derived from a clinical study focused on Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome (FIRES) patients and do not involve athletes, exercise interventions, or performance-related outcomes. Therefore, these specific findings regarding intracellular IL1RA isoforms in this context do not support direct interpretation related to training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated a 12-week supervised concurrent endurance and strength training intervention in 61 sedentary, healthy adults (aged 19-55 years, BMI 20-35 kg/m2). The training aimed to assess individual responses to exercise, health, performance, and recovery. The other study involved physically inactive patients with stable coronary heart disease, comparing a Psychodynamic Motivation and Training program, individualized exercise advice, and usual care. This second study lacks an athletic or performance context and focuses on clinical populations and secondary prevention.
Effect Summary: Following a 12-week concurrent endurance and strength training intervention in healthy, sedentary adults, Intracellular Water (ICW) significantly increased (p=0.007). This increase in ICW was more pronounced in participants with a TC genotype of the ACTN3 gene compared to those with a TT genotype (p=0.040). For the second study, Intracellular Water was assessed at baseline and six months, but no changes or effects were reported in the provided findings.
Sport Implications: Increased Intracellular Water (ICW) following a structured training intervention in previously sedentary, healthy individuals suggests a positive cellular adaptation to exercise, reflecting improved cellular hydration and muscle health. This enhanced cellular integrity is foundational for muscle function, metabolism, and overall physical performance. The finding that ACTN3 genotype influences the gain in ICW highlights the role of genetic factors in individual adaptive responses to training, which is crucial for understanding variability in training outcomes and potentially for personalized training strategies. This biomarker can therefore serve as an indicator of positive training adaptation and muscle health status. The second study provides no athletic context or reported effects for sports-specific interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated the effect of everolimus, an mTORC1 inhibitor, on tumor volume and growth rate in patients with progressive NF2-related vestibular schwannomas. Participants were adults and adolescents with a specific medical condition (Neurofibromatosis type 2), not athletes or individuals undergoing exercise interventions.
Effect Summary: Following everolimus treatment, one non-target intracranial meningioma in a participant showed a 9.6% reduction in volume at 6 months compared to baseline. In contrast, 11 out of 15 non-target tumors, including other meningiomas, remained stable in volume during the study period.
Sport Implications: This biomarker, which measures the volume of intracranial meningiomas and their response to medical treatment, has no direct relevance to understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. It is indicative of disease progression and treatment efficacy for a specific medical condition (NF2-related tumors) and does not provide insights into exercise physiology or sports performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This longitudinal observational study characterized host responses, cellular injury, and tissue damage in pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C).
Effect Summary: Plasma levels of intrahepatic cholangiocyte-derived cfRNA were observed to be increased in pediatric patients with high alanine transaminase (ALT) levels (above 36 U/L), indicating cholangiocyte (liver cell) injury or death.
Sport Implications: This study's findings are derived from a population of pediatric patients with COVID-19 and MIS-C, with no reported athletic context, training intervention, or exercise-related data. Therefore, the direct implications of intrahepatic cholangiocyte-derived cfRNA for understanding training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes cannot be determined from this research. The observed correlation with liver cell injury in a disease state does not provide a basis for athletic interpretation without further athletic-specific investigation.

Activity Context Summary: Twenty healthy recreational runners performed a 10-km treadmill run at a moderate speed (10-12 km/h) while wearing knee-high compression stockings (25 mmHg) or without them. Measurements were taken during rest, the run, and post-run recovery.
Effect Summary: Wearing knee-high compression stockings significantly elevated intramuscular pressure (IMP) in the tibialis anterior muscle at rest (24 ± 1.1 mmHg higher), during a 10-km treadmill run (22 ± 3.1 mmHg higher on average), and throughout the post-run recovery period. Concomitantly, muscle tissue oxygenation was reduced, and serum myoglobin increased, while creatine kinase levels remained unchanged.
Sport Implications: Intramuscular Pressure (IMP) is a relevant biomarker for understanding localized mechanical stress and its impact on muscle physiology in athletes. Elevated IMP, as observed with compression stocking use during and after exercise, indicates increased pressure within muscle compartments. This can compromise muscle tissue oxygenation, potentially increasing metabolic stress during training and hindering performance by limiting oxygen delivery. The concurrent increase in myoglobin suggests early muscle damage, adding to the acute training stress. Persistently elevated IMP and reduced oxygenation post-exercise could potentially impair recovery processes by affecting nutrient delivery and waste removal, thereby influencing overall adaptation and an athlete's ability to recover effectively from training loads.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study was a large-scale observational analysis involving 5522 individuals from general population cohorts (FHS, JHS, WHI, MESA). It investigated associations between Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) and epigenetic age acceleration, including IEAA, with clinical outcomes like all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease (CHD). No therapeutic intervention or specific activity type was administered; it was an epidemiological study of genetic and epigenetic markers.
Effect Summary: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) was significantly associated with Intrinsic Epigenetic Age Acceleration (IEAA), corresponding to an acceleration of 2.92 years. IEAA serves as an indicator of biological aging, and its acceleration is strongly linked to CHIP. The combination of CHIP and significant epigenetic age acceleration (including IEAA) identifies a high-risk population for clinical outcomes such as all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease.
Sport Implications: The provided study is a large-scale observational study on a general population, investigating associations between Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) and epigenetic age acceleration (including IEAA) with clinical outcomes like all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease. There is no athletic or exercise context reported. Therefore, this finding does not directly provide insights into training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in athletes. Speculation on its direct relevance to athletic performance or training load monitoring would be outside the scope of the provided data.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The context is immune monitoring programs for patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) and cellular therapies, focusing on immune reconstitution and preventing complications like graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).
Effect Summary: Higher invariant Natural Killer T cell (iNKT) reconstitution post-allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) correlates with improved patient outcomes. Elevated iNKT cell levels within the graft are linked to subsequent increased numbers in HCT recipients, and higher iNKT-containing graft doses are associated with a reduced incidence of acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD). iNKT cells possess diverse immunologic functions, including the ability to suppress T-cell proliferation and IFN-γ production.
Sport Implications: The provided findings are entirely focused on immune monitoring in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and cellular therapies. There is no athletic context or information related to training stress, recovery, adaptation, or performance in athletes. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation concerning exercise physiology, training load monitoring, or athletic performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study focuses on the development and optimization of a portable biosensor for rapid thrombin activity detection, where invertase serves as a component of the in vitro enzymatic assay.
Effect Summary: Invertase concentration, used as a signal transducer in a biosensor, decreases in solution as thrombin activity increases, due to its encapsulation within a fibrin hydrogel. This decrease is proportional to thrombin activity, and an optimal concentration of 1.0 mg/mL was utilized in the assay to catalyze sucrose hydrolysis into glucose and fructose.
Sport Implications: The study describes invertase's role as an exogenous enzyme within a diagnostic assay for thrombin activity. It is not presented as an endogenous biomarker whose levels or activity in an athlete are responsive to training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery. Therefore, these findings do not provide direct sport-specific implications regarding physiological responses to exercise or training.

Activity Context Summary: Elite male rowers (n=16) underwent two trials, each involving two strenuous 90-minute non-weight-bearing rowing ergometer sessions (90-100% of 2 mmol·L−1 capillary blood lactate power) separated by 150 minutes. The intervention involved acute preexercise consumption of either a high calcium meal (~1000 mg) or an isocaloric low calcium meal (<10 mg) before training.
Effect Summary: During repeated strenuous exercise, ionized calcium (iCa) concentrations decreased significantly in the low calcium intake group, being approximately 4.5% lower than the high calcium group after the first exercise session and 2.4% lower after the second. Conversely, a high preexercise calcium meal intake maintained iCa concentrations above the low calcium group for a sustained period of approximately 7 hours, encompassing both exercise and recovery periods.
Sport Implications: Monitoring ionized calcium provides insight into an athlete's physiological response to training stress, particularly in sports involving sustained strenuous effort. A decline in iCa indicates a disruption in calcium homeostasis, which can trigger endocrine responses like increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) release and heightened bone resorption. For athletes, especially those engaged in non-weight-bearing or high-volume training, maintaining stable iCa levels through preexercise nutritional strategies appears to be a critical factor in mitigating acute bone turnover responses and supporting long-term bone health, thereby potentially reducing the risk of bone stress injuries. Furthermore, stable iCa levels are fundamental for optimal muscle contraction and nerve transmission, suggesting that nutritional support to maintain iCa could contribute to sustained physiological function and performance capacity during prolonged exercise and aid in recovery by supporting overall musculoskeletal integrity.

Activity Context Summary: Both studies utilized mouse models of neurological conditions. One study investigated traumatic brain injury (TBI) and the effects of various pharmacological and genetic interventions (e.g., neutrophil extracellular trap inhibition, STING modulation, PAD4 overexpression) on neuroinflammation. The other study explored stem cell therapy (mesenchymal and neural stem cells) in transgenic mouse models of Alzheimer's disease and glioblastoma. No athlete or exercise context is reported in either study.
Effect Summary: Iba-1 protein expression and the number of Iba-1-positive microglia/macrophages were significantly increased in the brain (contused cortex) of mice following traumatic brain injury (TBI). This increase was further exacerbated by PAD4 overexpression and STING activation. Conversely, treatment with a neutrophil extracellular trap inhibitor (Cl-amidine) or a STING antagonist (C-176) significantly reduced the TBI-induced elevation of Iba-1-positive microglia/macrophages. In a separate study, Iba-1 protein levels and microglial cell counts in the brain of Alzheimer's disease mouse models remained unchanged following intranasal administration of mesenchymal stem cells.
Sport Implications: Iba-1 serves as a marker for microglia/macrophage presence and activation, primarily within the central nervous system, reflecting a neuroinflammatory response. The provided findings are derived exclusively from animal models of acute brain injury and chronic neurodegenerative diseases. As such, these data do not directly relate to exercise physiology, training stress, recovery processes, or athletic performance in healthy human athletes. There is no information presented to indicate how Iba-1 levels might be modulated by exercise, contribute to adaptation, signal underrecovery, or predict performance outcomes in an athletic context.

Activity Context Summary: One study investigated Irisin in a non-athletic context, focusing on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients, including diagnostic assessment and preoperative evaluation for hepatectomy. Another study involved healthy male volunteers undergoing resistance exercise to induce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), with some receiving nutritional supplementation (NPN_1) to assess its effect on recovery.
Effect Summary:
In the non-athletic context of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), Irisin gene expression (FNDC5/Irisin) was significantly downregulated in HCC tissues, and serum Irisin protein levels were lower in HCC patients compared to healthy controls. Low preoperative serum Irisin levels in HCC patients correlated with higher postoperative complication scores and longer hospital stays after hepatectomy.

In the athletic context, serum/plasma Irisin concentration transiently and significantly increased immediately following resistance exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) in healthy males, returning to baseline within two hours. Increased Irisin expression was specifically recorded in the group supplemented with NPN_1.
Sport Implications: Irisin's acute and transient increase immediately following resistance exercise-induced muscle damage (DOMS) in healthy individuals suggests its role as an acute exercise response marker. Given its involvement in energy metabolism, muscle adaptations, and glycogenesis, this response may indicate active metabolic signaling related to glycogen replenishment and muscle repair/regeneration processes during early recovery. The observation that Irisin expression was modulated in the group receiving a supplement known to improve strength recovery and reduce fatigue further implies its potential as a biomarker for assessing acute training stress, recovery status, and the effectiveness of recovery interventions. Its reported function of 'indicating muscle tissue injury' reinforces its relevance in monitoring the physiological impact of training and potentially guiding recovery strategies. The findings from hepatocellular carcinoma studies do not provide direct athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: This biomarker was investigated in various athletic populations and contexts: rowers subjected to exhaustive exercise with 6-week cranberry extract supplementation; young professional long-distance and sprint swimmers during a 10-week preparatory training period for recovery monitoring; elite professional soccer players over an 11-month competitive season (post-match recovery, intense training, player position differences); and elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race with 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation. General athletes, especially females, were also considered in a review of biomarker-guided monitoring. One study examined healthy older adults during 14 days of head-down bed rest with a multimodal exercise countermeasure. Two studies had no athletic context, focusing on diabetic nephropathy or age-related macular degeneration.
Effect Summary: Serum/plasma iron levels exhibit dynamic responses to exercise and training. Post-exhaustive exercise, serum iron can significantly increase. During prolonged intensive training periods (e.g., soccer seasons), plasma iron may show a decreasing trend, particularly in highly active positions (midfielders/defenders), though fluctuations also occur with season and cumulative game time. In swimmers during preparatory training, recovery plasma iron concentrations tended to increase. Iron deficiency is prevalent in athletes, especially females, and is characterized by insufficient serum ferritin. Oral iron supplementation (80 mg/day) effectively prevented a decline and maintained/increased serum iron levels in elite cyclists during a 3-week stage race, whereas control groups experienced declines. In a non-athletic context, serum iron decreased following 14 days of head-down bed rest. Other non-athletic findings noted iron deposition in kidney tissue of diabetic nephropathy patients and no significant difference in plasma levels in age-related macular degeneration patients.
Sport Implications:
Iron is an essential micronutrient critical for athletic performance, especially in endurance sports, due to its fundamental role in oxygen transport, hemoglobin formation, and aerobic energy metabolism. Monitoring serum/plasma iron, often alongside ferritin, is crucial for assessing an athlete's nutritional status and preventing iron deficiency, which can lead to fatigue, anemia, hindered training adaptations, impaired endurance performance, and increased susceptibility to infections.

Transient post-exercise elevations in iron may indicate acute physiological stress, potentially contributing to oxidative stress and inflammation, relevant for recovery strategies. Conversely, persistent low iron levels during intensive training or competitive seasons, particularly in athletes with high physical demands, suggest increased utilization, potential losses, or altered iron metabolism due to chronic stress. In these scenarios, iron deficiency can compromise performance and recovery.

Oral iron supplementation has been shown to be an effective strategy to prevent declines in iron status during periods of high training and competition, thereby supporting hematological profiles, enhancing athletic performance, improving endurance capacity, and potentially mitigating fatigue and muscle damage.

Reduced iron levels observed during periods of bed rest (detraining/deconditioning) highlight the importance of maintaining iron status during injury rehabilitation or periods of reduced activity to support recovery and preparation for return to sport. Findings from studies on diabetic nephropathy and age-related macular degeneration have no direct sport-specific implications.

Activity Context Summary: The context involves comprehensive blood biomarker profiling and monitoring in high-performance athletes to optimize physiology, nutrition, training, recovery, and prevent injury/illness. This includes managing energy availability, training load, and recovery, particularly in endurance athletes, and addressing iron deficiency via supplementation. Relevant scenarios include intense exercise, eccentric loading, single matches, long-haul travel, sleep loss, altitude training, and season-long competitive demands, with specific attention to female athletes and menstrual blood loss.
Effect Summary: Iron status markers (Iron, Ferritin, MCV, MCH, Reticulocytes, Hepcidin) are used to identify iron deficiency. Low iron status, especially severe deficiency (ferritin < 12 ng/mL), compromises erythropoiesis and reduces total hemoglobin mass (tHbmass), which is often 40% higher in endurance athletes. MCV and MCH indicate compromised red blood cell volume and hemoglobin content, while reticulocytes reflect recent erythropoietic activity and can signal compromised status. Hepcidin regulates iron absorption and homeostasis, and its levels interact with exercise, iron deficiency, and iron overload. Females are more susceptible to iron deficiency due to menstrual blood loss.
Sport Implications: Monitoring iron status is critical for high-performance athletes, particularly endurance athletes, to ensure optimal oxygen transport capacity and erythropoietic function. Low iron status impairs training tolerance, compromises adaptation to altitude training, and reduces endurance performance by limiting oxygen delivery. Severe iron deficiency directly reduces total hemoglobin mass (tHbmass), leading to sub-optimal maximal oxygen-carrying capacity and aerobic power. Hemoglobin concentration alone is an unreliable indicator of true oxygen-carrying capacity due to plasma volume shifts. Hepcidin provides valuable insights into an athlete's iron absorption efficiency, guiding targeted nutritional interventions. Regular monitoring, considering factors like menstrual blood loss in female athletes and training load, facilitates timely supplementation to optimize oxygen transport, support recovery, and enhance athletic performance.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. This study performed a proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells, human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), and their original somatic cells. The aim was to identify pluripotency markers and understand the proteomic profiles of stem cells.
Effect Summary: Isocitrate Dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) protein levels were consistently observed to be higher (up-regulated by >=1.5-fold) in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) compared to their respective somatic precursor cells (fibroblasts and peripheral blood mononuclear cells). This up-regulation was validated by Western blot analysis and was identified as a potential marker for stemness and pluripotency, with inferred involvement in cellular metabolism.
Sport Implications: The provided findings relate exclusively to the proteomic characterization of human stem cells (hiPSCs and hESCs) and their differentiation from somatic cells, identifying IDH1 as a marker associated with pluripotency and stemness maintenance. There is no information, experimental design, or context within this study that relates IDH1 levels or its function to exercise physiology, training stress, recovery, adaptation, or athletic performance. Therefore, these findings do not support any athletic interpretation within the specified domains.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The studies focus on primary human tumor data, primary AML blasts, inducible THP-1 cells, and glioma tissue in the context of cancer research and computational algorithm development for precision oncology.
Effect Summary: The IDH1-R132H mutation is a genetic alteration observed in various cancers, including lower-grade glioma and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This mutation is associated with increased expression of ACACA (acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha), a key enzyme in fatty acid synthesis. In IDH1-mutant AML, ACACA gene expression can be 1.5-2.0-fold higher. This increased expression leads to a synthetic lethal vulnerability, meaning that IDH1-mutant cells become selectively sensitive to ACACA inhibition (e.g., by TOFA), resulting in cell growth defects. Additionally, IDH1 mutations are noted to be related to survival outcomes in glioma when combined with TERT promoter mutations, generally conferring oncogenic properties due to their role as an altered metabolic enzyme.
Sport Implications: The provided findings relate exclusively to cancer biology, genetic alterations associated with oncogenesis, and potential therapeutic targets for cancer treatment. There is no information or context provided that links the IDH1 mutation or its observed effects (such as ACACA overexpression or sensitivity to inhibition) to training stress, adaptation, performance, recovery, metabolic flexibility in athletes, inflammation, muscle damage, or cardiovascular and endocrine adaptation in an athletic population. Therefore, these findings do not support an athletic interpretation.

Activity Context Summary: No athlete or exercise context reported. The study investigated healthy older adults undergoing 14 days of head-down bed rest (HDBR). One group received a multimodal exercise countermeasure (including high-intensity interval training, low-intensity cycling, or strength exercises) while the control group received passive physiotherapy, all performed in a head-down tilt or horizontal position.
Effect Summary: Isokinetic ankle dorsal flexion strength did not change with 14 days of head-down bed rest in either the exercise countermeasure group or the passive physiotherapy control group.
Sport Implications: This study's context (head-down bed rest in healthy older adults) is far removed from typical athletic training, competition, or recovery scenarios. While exercise was an intervention, its primary goal was to counteract deconditioning, not enhance athletic performance. The finding that ankle dorsiflexion strength remained unchanged during bed rest, unlike other strength parameters (e.g., knee extension strength), suggests a relative resilience of these specific muscles or movement patterns to the deconditioning effects of bed rest under these conditions. However, this does not directly inform training stress, adaptation, performance, or recovery in an athletic population actively engaged in sport.

Activity Context Summary: The study involved healthy older adults undergoing 14 days of continuous 6-degree head-down bed rest (HDBR). Participants were randomized to either a multimodal exercise countermeasure group (performing 3 sessions/day, 60-75 minutes total, including high-intensity interval training, low-intensity cycling, or strength exercises) or a control group receiving passive physiotherapy. All activities were completed in a head-down tilt or horizontal position. The context is the attenuation of musculoskeletal deconditioning and muscle strength loss during simulated microgravity/immobilization.
Effect Summary: Isokinetic ankle plantarflexion strength did not change with 14 days of head-down bed rest in either the multimodal exercise countermeasure group or the passive physiotherapy control group.
Sport Implications: In the context of this study (healthy older adults undergoing 14 days of head-down bed rest), the finding that isokinetic ankle plantarflexion strength remained unchanged in both exercise and control groups suggests that this specific muscle function may be relatively resilient to short-term deconditioning from immobilization, or that the interventions tested were insufficient to elicit a measurable change in this parameter. From a sports-science perspective, this biomarker in this specific context provides limited direct insight into typical training stress, adaptation, or performance optimization for actively training athletes. While the study explores countermeasures for deconditioning, a situation relevant to injured athletes, the lack of a measurable change limits its utility for informing specific training or recovery strategies in an athletic population. It indicates that these interventions did not significantly impact dynamic ankle plantarflexion strength under these specific deconditioning conditions.

Activity Context Summary: This study investigated healthy older adults subjected to 14 days of continuous 6-degree Head-Down Bed Rest (HDBR), a model for musculoskeletal deconditioning. One group received a multimodal exercise countermeasure (3 sessions/day, 60-75 minutes total, including high-intensity interval training, low-intensity cycling, or strength exercises for lower/upper body) while the control group received passive physiotherapy. The exercise intervention aimed to attenuate deconditioning, not to induce athletic training adaptations.
